articles.title: xTool M2 color craft laser and engraver review: Improved print head and positioning cameras at a lower price
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The xTool M2 color craft laser and engraver brings crafting flexibility at a new low price while improving on several features, at the expense of the cutting blade and pen options offered by the M1.
Pros
- +New $549 entry price
- +Twin positioning cameras
- +Air assist integrated
- +Black ink added to print process
- +xTool Studio is generally good software
- +Fully enclosed with built-in extractor fan
- +10W diode, 20W diode, CMYK, 2W IR laser head options
Cons
- -Extras can soon push the price beyond $1,000
- -Non-refillable ink cart costs $99 to replace
- -Cutting base is just a flat metal tray
- -Provided magnetic material standoff clamps are flimsy
- -A few operational wrinkles
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Here’s xTool’s second take on an all-in-one craft tool in a box. It isn’t just an iterative update to the xTool M1 Ultra. The new XTool M2 color craft laser and engraver thoroughly remixes the offering. Specifically, it throws out the previous model’s cutting blade and pen options. To compensate, it comes with a 10W diode, a 20W diode, CMYK, and a 2W IR laser head, “cut, print, engrave” options. Very worthy improvements, such as positioning and monitoring cameras, come as standard this time around. Furthermore, the print head offers CMYK inks instead of the washed-out CMY of yore, and laser air assist is included as standard. xTool’s new M2 also works with the RA3 Lite full wrap rotary accessory.
The xTool M2 10W base model is available for $599. This entry price makes the M2 about half the price of last year’s M1 Ultra. But this 10W ‘Standalone’ bundle includes just the machine and a 10W diode laser head. You’ll have to part with $699 (usually $749) for the 10W ‘Color Print & Cut Bundle’, which includes the CMYK print head and a cartridge. Moving up to $939 (usually $989) gets you the 10W Deluxe Bundle.
There are also bundles with the 20W diode laser head costing $400 more per tier (Standard, Color Print & Cut, and Deluxe). xTool also sells various print/cut heads separately, and they’re easily magnetically swappable. For example, it lists the M2 CMYK printing module with an ink cartridge for $169, extra cartridges are $99, and the RA3 Lite is $259. We don’t have prices for a 20W diode head (if you wanted to upgrade later), nor the 3W IR laser head that is shown on the promotional pages for the product.
You might prefer the 20W diode laser for faster, deeper cuts. xTool says it raises the max basswood cutting depth from 8mm to 10mm in one pass. For acrylic, it is much better, raising the cutting thickness from 3mm to 8mm in one pass with the 20W diode laser installed.
The default 10W diode laser supplied will be good enough for cutting and engraving plenty of materials for many crafty users. Officially, the following tabulated materials are cuttable, engravable, and printable.
| Compatible materials |  | 
|---|---|
| Cuttable | Wood / Opaque Acrylic / Paper / Cardstock / Cardboard / Foam / MDF / Leather / Felt | 
| Engravable | Wood / Opaque Acrylic / Transparent Acrylic / Leather / Stainless Steel / Aluminum / Plated Metal / Paper / MDF / Cardboard / Felt / Rubber / Glass / Plastic / Cork / Ceramic | 
| Printable | Paper / Cardstock / Sticker Paper / Wood / Canvas / Fabric / Felt / Leather / Glass | 
You will see examples of cutting, engraving, and printing on various materials during our test process below.
As mentioned, the newest Color Craft machine from xTool improves on the older and more expensive model by integrating a pair of positioning and monitoring cameras. There’s also a separate camera for fire hazard monitoring and alerts. Another improvement on the original comes via the integration of air assist for the laser. Fan-powered extraction, with corrugated flexible extendable pipe, is another welcome new standard feature. As with the previous model, we have a laser-safe tinted enclosure lid, which should mean your eyes are adequately protected when the machine runs with the lid closed.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Finally, the newest Color Craft laser from xTool now comes with the excellent xTool Studio software we last used alongside the formidable xTool P3. This is a comprehensive package for laser control and output, as well as for guiding you through wizards, generators, apps, and plenty of projects online. Most projects I completed went easily, from photo and/or illustration and layout to output. I did hit a couple of bugs, but more on that later.
Specifications: xTool M1 Ultra
| Machine Footprint | 24.4 x 20.5 x 9.8 inches | 
| Engraving Size | 16.7 x 12.5 inches (425 x 318mm) | 
| CMYK Print Size | 13.7 x 11.8 inches (348 x 300mm) | 
| Materials | Wood, paper, leather, fabric, felt, vinyl, cardboard, coated metals (engrave), plastics, etc. | 
| Laser Type | 455nm diode laser | 
| Laser Power | 10W or 20W diode modules | 
| Optional Modules | CMYK print head, 2W IR laser head | 
| Engraving Accuracy | 0.01mm positioning precision | 
| Cutting Platform | Removable flat metal tray, 4x magnetic standoffs provided | 
| Connectivity | USB‑C · Wi-Fi | 
| Interface | Dual‑camera preview · auto‑alignment · xTool Studio software | 
| Safety | Class 1 enclosure · lid‑open stop · emergency stop · flame detection camera | 
| Dimensions | 24.4 x 20.5 x 9.8 inches | 
| Weight | ~22 pounds | 
| MSRP | $599 10W $999 20W | 
| Release Date | May 27, 2026 | 
xTool M2: Included in the Box
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The device was well packed, with everything padded and secured nicely for transportation. Moreover, it won’t be that tricky to get it back in the box as it is a simple shape with no machine assembly required.
In addition to the desktop laser chassis, we got the 10W diode head, a power brick and IEC cable with region-appropriate plug, a USB cable to connect a computer (need to set up by cable before using Wi-Fi), a short USB cable to connect the accessory head to the magnetic holder on the gantry, some grease for the transport system, a USB-A to –C adaptor, a hex-driver, masking tape, and a few pieces of material for setup, calibration, and test.
We got the 10W Deluxe Bundle (though in several deliveries, not boxed together). We received the print head and cartridge, the rotary tool, and a few more slivers of sample material.
Design of the xTool M2
xTool has designed the M2 as a fully enclosed box with a laser-safe orange-tinted acrylic top. The machine only operates with the lid closed.
You open the lid to position your work within the 16.7 x 12.5 inches (425 x 318 mm) lasering area. However, please be aware that for multi-stage color craft projects, where you will want to swap between laser and CMYK print heads, the print area is a smaller 13.7 x 11.8 inches (348 x 300 mm). I didn’t have any size/area mismatch surprises during my projects as the software preview made one aware of the overall working areas available.
Swapping tool heads is quick and simple. The heads are magnetic, guided accurately and firmly into place by a trio of short metal rods. Then you connect the provided USB-C cable, which is the perfect length for the job. xTool Studio software is smart enough to know what kind of head is installed, and you should switch to it in the midst of multi-step processes.
A big convenient step up from the prior generation is the integration of cameras into the new machine. There’s one camera in the center of the lid to snap the whole of the bed. Meanwhile, the machine’s gantry-attached head also has a camera on one side, and you can use it for closer detail shots and/or monitoring the cutting/printing work. There’s actually a third camera in one corner, but that is devoted to flame detection. A couple of times during testing, that flame detection paused a job I was working on, with a loud beep. However, checking and resuming didn’t seem to have any impact on the finished job’s quality or accuracy.
The cameras also integrate with xTool Studio to focus correctly on the workpiece surface, and to provide auto-material detection. That second feature works best with xTool-supplied materials which come with a QR code so the software knows exactly what the material properties are.
Other good things about the new M2, compared to the predecessor, are the built-in air assist, which can help with clean engraving and deeper cuts, as well as the provision of a new print head with a dedicated black ink tank. The extra black ink should improve the contrast of the print output and make it closer in quality to a decent modern inkjet printer. We will see about that later in the review.
Assembling the xTool M2
Commissioning the xTool M2 was pleasingly simple. The unit came out of the box fully assembled. All a buyer has to do is carefully take off all the peels and remove strips of tape that hold the lid and other parts in place, and after that, it will be almost ready to go.
Once I got it on the desk, I opened the lid and took out the bits and pieces of xTool supplies to get the machine set up. Everything I needed was here for setup, including USB cables, grease for the gantry movement mechanism, a screwdriver, an exhaust pipe, and various materials that are used during calibration.
With everything plugged in and powered up, and connected to the computer, the xTool Studio software guides you through initial calibration for the magnetically attached head you have installed. As ours came with the 10W diode head in the first package, I calibrated this by following the ‘wizard’ style step-by-step process. It was easy enough to subsequently find the calibration menu again the next day, when the CMYK print module arrived.
Safety Precautions for the xTool M2
We’ve already mentioned that the M2 claims to be Class 1 safe, with its enclosed design stopping accidental exposure to unhindered Class 4 diode laser light. xTool provides documentation and online guidance that users are encouraged to check out to ensure safe operation. Do not try to override the built-in safety, as the diode laser within could damage eyes and burn skin.
Another safety issue with lasers is addressed with the third camera we mentioned previously. This corner camera monitors smoke and flames, which can flare up when some materials are engraved or cut.
Lasers can also create toxic fumes, depending on what they’re engraving and/or cutting. While you can hook up the xTool M2 to various workshop extraction and filtering equipment, it is good that it comes as standard with a powered fan and flexible extending corrugated exhaust pipe. When I positioned my xTool M2 test unit, it was convenient to shove that corrugated hose out of the window. It worked very well during testing, evacuating smoke made when cutting materials quickly and effectively. The exhaust fan is smartly controlled by xTool Studio, which auto-adjusts speed and duration of operation.
Software for xTool M2
Just like with the xTool P3 and the F2 Ultra, the new xTool M2 color craft laser and engraver is designed to work with the free bundled xTool Studio software. The software looks and works like many other bundled laser software suites for engraving, scoring, and cutting tasks, easily applying multiple output settings across several project layers. The familiar illustration style primitives and type handling might be good enough for creating some projects from scratch, but you can also make use of wizard-like apps to guide you through popular tasks like making arrays and grids, and other repeating designs, as well as more complex projects like boxes and jigsaws.
Traditional software-based graphic creating tools are augmented in xTool Studio with AI-driven generators, custom apps, as well as convenient in-UI access to large online project libraries, notably Atomm.
Of course, the xTool Studio software handles the multi-stage workflows that products like the M2 enable. Making hybrid projects that mix color graphic printing, laser engraving, and cutting was a cinch. The software also works great with accessories you might add to xTool M2 bundles like the rotary accessory, and probably the UV laser head (which we didn't get to test this time).
Engraving / Cutting with the xTool M2
Now comes the fun part. I prepared a number of projects that I thought would adequately test the cutting, engraving, and printing prowess of the new xTool M2 color craft laser and engraver, to give it its full title. I started with the laser-toting fan favorite of a plywood surface engrave test.
I got a piece of xTool’s 3mm birch ply, which provides a pale and characterless wood surface for engraving detail and is pretty quick to cut cleanly, even with a 10W diode laser. The first job on the M2 was to output the usual variable speed and power engraving test grid. This provides a good visual light-to-dark shading guide for any later pale wood projects. There are quite a few usable shades here, even at the fastest speed of up to 600 mm/s. The xTool M1 Ultra was limited to 300 mm/s at best.
xTool Studio made setting up the test grid easy with a click-and-go generator. However, my first burn seemed to use the same settings for every ‘X’ so I had to select and type in the appropriate values for each segment and output it again. Thus the generator wasn’t much of a labor saver. Hopefully this bug will be fixed in due course.
I stuck with pure laser output for my first tests. I’ll do CMYK printing and hybrid jobs later. So the next thing I did was try a simple line art engrave onto a slate coaster. You can see the result of this in the images - a stylized silhouette of a tree on stone. The output is very pleasing, and it worked like this first shot using the xTool M2’s rock coaster engraving preset. I didn’t do any special surface preparation or finishing. I just cleaned the slate with a brush before setting off the M2 engrave process.
Next up, I got out my painted aluminum business card blanks. The red one you see in the images was created with the xTool M2. It looks nice and sharp at first glance. Only when you zoom in to high-res images can you see a slight resolution advantage on the black card, which was engraved when I tested the xTool P3 CO2 laser. The red card has slight jaggies under scrutiny.
Satisfied with the engraving so far, I felt it would be good to look more closely at the new CMYK print capabilities. Using art paper supplied by xTool, I printed a colorful flower picture, which you can see positioned in my photo next to the same image on my laptop’s lovely OLED screen. The printed output lacks contrast and pop in comparison, but to be fair to xTool, I hadn’t used special (glossy finish and high-white) photo paper, which would squeeze the best print quality from this kind of inkjet printer module.
What about comparing the xTool CMYK output to a professional lithographic print I had produced a few years back (2007!)? You can see my original illustrated menu was printed on a nice heavy card stock by commercial firm Priority Print. I’d actually say that the xTool’s output is just as nice, but would benefit from being a bit darker/denser. Both prints came from the same PDF file. Apologies for the black circle on the xTool M2’s printout, that’s from a calibration I did earlier.
With two comparison prints produced so far, if I were a perfectionist I’d be tempted to adjust the levels of the xTool print output to be a bit darker and up the contrast.
Now let’s use some of the hybrid output ability of the xTool M2. I saw a project in the xTool Studio library with a wood version of tic tac toe (noughts & crosses) but thought it looked a bit basic, so I fired up Illustrator to make a nicer stylized version, which I dubbed Fridge Tac Toe. I intended to add magnetic pads to the cutout shapes and board and make the game fridge-friendly.
The M2 outputs the color sections with its CMYK head. It then asked me to change to the laser head, and proceeded to cut the shapes, followed by the board. There were a couple of processing wrinkles, but I salvaged the project without issues. Specifically, the laser cut around the inner rounded rectangles twice, and that action accidentally lasered some pieces that had already dropped onto the bed. I’m not sure if it was my source file at issue, the settings, or a software bug. Thankfully, I had decided to cut some spare O's and X's.
Slightly more ambitious, I decided to make a jigsaw from one of my favorite holiday photos. The xTool software generated this for me once fed an image. All I had to do, I thought, was make sure to position it carefully within the common area where printing and lasering can be achieved.
As you can see from my jigsaw-making gallery, the first attempt wasted a sheet of plywood and plenty of ink. For some reason with this first attempt, the jigsaw lines were printed on top of the image – not necessary. Also, the run order ruined the project. The machine cut the outer frame of the jigsaw first. This caused the center (what would have become the jigsaw pieces) to fall immediately down onto the metal bed, which is about 6 or 7 mm lower than the standoffs that had been holding the wood sheet up. Thus the laser wasn’t focused to cut, and even if it had been capable of cutting, we’d get a lot of burn on the back of the piece due to a lack of air gap under the work.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
After aborting the beach photo jigsaw, I picked another holiday photo featuring a yacht and ran the jigsaw generator again. This time I edited the resulting project work on the xTool Studio canvas. I selected the outer frame cut and made sure it would be the last action of the laser by putting it on its own last-in-order layer. This ensured the layers would be processed in the following order: photo print, jigsaw pieces cut, jigsaw pieces outer frame cut. This worked nicely, with a very handsome and accurately cut working jigsaw at the end. Using a ‘honeycomb’ cutting bed would have been better for this style of job.
Another hybrid job I output was some stickers for the grandkids. These cartoon illustration versions of photos were generated by an AI tool, and I used the xTool Studio to generate offset cutting forms to match each one.
I couldn’t find a preset for this kind of sticker cut out in the xTool software. That was a surprise, as I saw lots of stickers in promotional material. Anyway, printing looked great, and my guestimated laser cutting using one pass at 15% power and 15mm/s speed was perfect. It cut the stickers cleanly without cutting the backing material.
My final project made use of the supplied RA3 Lite rotary accessory. It was a bit fiddly to install and it meant fixing a different magnetic head adapter to change the orientation of the printer / laser (see images). Also, the xTool M2’s camera positioning functions stopped being useful when in this mode.
I planned to engrave some terracotta plant pots, one for pencils, one for herbs. So, I prepared some line art logos for this labeling purpose, and then imported them into xTool Studio. There I selected the rotary output option for the M2, and followed the steps to measure the usable (engravable) surface and its slope / profile.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Multiple grip adaptors are provided with the RA3 Lite rotary chuck, so I could turn the work around and then engrave the plant pot rim. That was an important technique to get used to, because you can’t engrave close up to the chuck. I think the user-addressable zone of the work in the chuck starts about an inch away from the chuck jaws, probably to prevent head/chuck jaw collisions.
Finally, I got some pretty nice results with the laser engraving of terracotta, so I’m pleased with the handsome textured finish which you can see in my gallery.
Bottom Line
I found the xTool M2 to be a great one-stop shop for craft projects. Most of the ideas I had for cool things to make went from ideation to finished output with very little friction from the machine or bundled software. Lots and lots more projects using a far wider range of materials (check the above chart) are possible. Moreover, xTool Studio’s built-in generators, AI, and integration with project libraries via Atomm make it easy to get more inspiration even if you don’t paint, illustrate, or DIY design.
From looking at the print samples from the M1 Ultra, I’m certain the CMYK output from the M2 is much better and more usable for hobbyists. If you were to do a lot of print work, or something like a production run, I think it would be worthwhile tweaking to optimize contrast, though. Remember it is inkjet, too, so the print surface makes a lot of difference, and you may have to lacquer the surface after printing to make it moderately splash-proof.
The entry-level pricing of $599 looks like a good move from xTool. Adding $150 for the CMYK head and a cartridge doesn’t seem exorbitant – until you realize ink refills are $99. This so-called ‘Color Print and Cut Bundle’ makes the most sense to get the best of the xTool M2’s most attractive features from day one.
While the 10W (default) and 20W diode laser heads are very flexible across use cases and materials, those with a particular interest in metal projects (and some plastic types) might like to add the 3W IR laser head. I’ve heard that’s an extra $499, though, so you’d really have to have a few important projects in mind to pay almost the same price as the M2 laser alone.
The xTool M2 deserves a place in our list of the Best Laser Cutters and Engravers. However, if the added flexibility of this all-in-one print and cut machine isn’t something that tempts you, there may be better choices. For example, our recommended xTool S1 with a 40W diode laser head can get things done quicker and cut deeper for not a lot more than the M2 20W.
Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: How to take better photos of your pets
articles.text:
Like the pets of any self-respecting millennial, my cats have their own Instagram account.
How to take better photos of your pets
Tips and tricks to get your pet looking their best.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Noodle and Loaf — aka Carb Cats — aren’t exactly celebrities. But they are used to having their photos taken a lot. Between their Instagram account, my regular need to test smartphone cameras, and the fact that they are two adorable idiots, I’ve taken on an unofficial household role as pet photographer.
I know I’m not the only one. It’s become standard practice to maintain a camera roll full of blurry bleps and dozing dogs. But pets are rarely easy to photograph. They’re usually small, fast, and don’t take direction well. Here are a few ways to improve your odds.
The hardware
Most of the photos I take are because one of the cats is doing something cute right now, and so the best camera for the job is the one I have on me. That’s usually my phone, which is how I’ve taken the overwhelming majority of my pet photos, with a handful more shot on film.
A good camera will certainly bring advantages, and I wouldn’t want to put anyone off getting into the hobby. In this case, a better phone camera might be more beneficial though — and is probably cheaper.
If you really do want to make an investment, the best bang for your buck is in lighting. I have a cheap $40 softbox light from Raleno, originally purchased for the sake of taking product photos, but occasionally repurposed with the cats in mind. The extra light helps bring out details and stops indoor shots from looking too flat or too yellow, common issues when you’re reliant on regular household lights. It can be useful for the occasional staged shot (easier with some pets than others), but won’t help much with candids.
The settings
I also mostly shoot in the default camera mode. What can I say? I’m lazy. That may work just fine for you too, but if you want to dive into specific shooting modes or play with settings manually, there are some tweaks worth making.
The big one is shutter speed. Most pets aren’t great at sitting still, and you’re probably used to taking photos that are ruined by motion blur. The quickest fix is a faster shutter speed, which shortens the exposure time to capture sharper shots of moving subjects. Many Android camera apps have a dedicated sports mode, which does this for you — how much difference is there really between a professional athlete and a cat with zoomies?
iPhones don’t have a sports mode, but instead you can try burst mode, which you’ll also find on most Androids. It takes a bunch of photos in quick succession with short shutter speeds, perfect for when you’re trying to catch a dog mid-run or a cat darting after a toy, giving you a selection of action shots to choose from.
The caveat is that shorter shutter speeds mean less light capture. That’s usually fine in bright daylight, but in dimmer lighting — and sometimes even simply if you’re indoors — quality will drop. I took this shot of Noodle trying to grab a toy using burst mode, and it captured her crisply but introduced a whole lot of noise into the black parts of my computer displays behind her.
You might also want to think about aperture. Pet photos are just like any portrait and often benefit from a blurred background that helps draw attention to the subject. Phones can add this bokeh effect through portrait mode, but if you’re tweaking manually, then dropping the aperture will get the right result. Just don’t drop it too far — most pets have deeper faces than humans, and too wide an aperture risks leaving their nose in focus while the ears are blurry. Somewhere between f/4 and f/5.6 is about right; play around to find what works.
Switching to a telephoto lens, whether on a real camera or on your phone, can help a portrait pop a little more, and has the added bonus of letting you shoot from a distance, reducing the odds that you’ll ruin the moment in your attempt to get close. Check if your phone has a dedicated telephoto lens — zooming in on the main camera won’t have the same effect.
Drop to eye level
Hardware and software aside, what about technique?
The single biggest improvement you can make is to get on their level. Don’t shoot your pet from standing; pop a squat and take a photo from head-on, just like you would if you were photographing a person. There’s nothing cuter than capturing big puppy-dog eyes up close.
If that’s tricky for whatever reason, try to snatch photos when your pets are elevated. My cats love to nap in raised radiator beds, and I used to photograph my parents’ Chihuahuas while they slept on the staircase. For reptiles, rodents, and other pets in tanks or cages, this is often easier, though shooting through the glass or bars will have an impact on quality. Take them out of the tank if that’s feasible.
Shots from standing can work, but it’s rare. Your photos look less considered and lower effort, and it’s much harder to frame them against a good backdrop or get that bokeh blur.
Break out the toys and treats
Even a free-spirited pet can be manipulated a little. Treats and toys are the best ways to maneuver most animals into position and control their attention.
Eye contact is one of the easiest ways to upgrade a photo, and for that you need to get your pet looking into the lens. My go-to is shaking a rattly, colorful toy directly above the camera (or asking my partner to do it for me). Cats are tricky because they get bored quickly, so you might need a variety of toys within easy reach to keep their attention.
Direct eye contact can produce brilliant photos, but some of my favorites have the cats looking off at an angle. The key is to make sure you’re still capturing their eyes, whether it’s head-on or not, and that they’re looking roughly toward the brightest light around.
Treat them like a wild animal
One of the classic mistakes is treating pets like kids: a little unpredictable but fundamentally capable of being controlled. Instead, treat them like wild animals.
Don’t go breaking out a pith helmet just yet, but try to photograph them on their own terms. You know when your dog is likely to be sleepy, so get that dozy shot when it’s naptime. If your cat loves to sprawl in sunbeams, wait for the light to get right and let them pose themselves. Noodle and Loaf always get the zoomies at night, so I know that’s when to nab playtime photos. You’ll know your own pets best, so plan around their habits.
My view on this is obviously shaped by owning cats, and before them several badly trained Chihuahuas. If you have a pet that’s better at following instructions, then by all means take advantage.
Either way, you’re guaranteed to take a load of terrible photos. You’ll get blurry ones because they moved too fast. You’ll get derpy ones because they yawned at just the wrong moment. You’ll get more direct shots of their ass than you’re entirely comfortable with.
Accept these facts. Make your peace with the bad shots and the buttholes, because you’ll have to get through them to get the perfect photo. And hey, sometimes the derpy ones end up being your favorites anyway.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Si eres programador, esta nueva IA de Microsoft es más rápida y barata que Claude Code
articles.text:
Microsoft ha lanzado una nueva IA para competir con Claude Code y otros modelos de desarrollo de software. Conocido como MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, el modelo está pensado para tareas de programación dentro de GitHub Copilot. Según sus creadores, esta IA supera en calidad, velocidad y coste a su predecesor y puede hacer frente a otros modelos de la industria.
MAI-Code-1.1-Flash llega como reemplazo al modelo que lanzó Microsoft durante la pasada Build 2026. En una publicación de su blog, el gigante tecnológico asegura que esta versión produce código de mayor calidad, consume menos tokens y cuesta una cuarta parte de lo que costaba el modelo anterior.
En términos generales, MAI-Code-1.1-Flash es un modelo pequeño y eficiente que se desempeña bien en tareas rápidas e iterativas a la hora de programar. Microsoft menciona que priorizó dos áreas que los desarrolladores señalaron como relevantes, y son la línea de comandos y el rendimiento en proyectos .NET. De acuerdo con los primeros benchmarks, esta versión consigue una mejora del 22% en Terminal-Bench 2.1 y 15% en otras tareas relacionadas con .NET.
Para evitar problemas con otras empresas, Microsoft entrenó MAI-Code-1.1-Flash desde cero, con datos propios y trazables. Los ingenieros aseguran que no usaron destilación de modelos de terceros, una técnica que ya se volvió popular entre las empresas chinas que intentan hacer frente a OpenAI y Anthropic.
Dejando de lado los benchmarks, Microsoft afirma que su nuevo modelo tiene lo suficiente para brillar en el entorno real. Según los datos de producción, la tasa de supervivencia del código aumentó un 4%, mientras que las visitas recurrentes de los desarrolladores subieron un 9%. La primera métrica tiene que ver con cuánto código generado por la IA se mantiene tras la edición y en el momento del commit.
¿Por qué deberías usar MAI-Code-1.1-Flash para programar?
Una ventaja puntual de MAI-Code-1.1-Flash es su eficiencia. La tecnológica menciona que los tokens se generan un 25% más rápido en GitHub Copilot y que el modelo necesita un 25% menos para completar una tarea. Los programadores obtendrán respuestas más veloces y un mejor aprovechamiento de cada token consumido, todo esto sin necesidad de cambiar a un modelo más grande.
A primera vista, todo suena muy bien, pero... ¿Qué tal se desempeña frente a otros modelos de IA? Para medir el rendimiento de MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, Microsoft revisó los datos de VS Code para evaluar la calidad del código y la eficiencia con la que se alcanzaba un resultado estable. Tras el análisis, la compañía encontró que su IA genera código de mayor calidad que Claude Haiku 4.5 y GPT-5.4 Mini.
Si lo ponemos a competir con GPT-5.6 Luna o Kimi K2.7 Code, MAI-Code-1-Flash no puede hacerles frente en calidad, pero sí en eficiencia. Estos modelos requieren entre un 67% y un 94% más de tokens por turno, además de que son necesarios más turnos para llegar a un commit. La IA de Microsoft puede ser más eficiente que Codex o Claude Code, pero estos mantienen la superioridad en términos de contexto y multimodalidad.
Microsoft menciona que MAI-Code-1.1-Flash está diseñado para trabajos ligeros, como explorar código existente, aplicar cambios, refinar pruebas y corregir errores. La longitud de respuesta se adaptará según la complejidad de la tarea, por lo que solo profundizará cuando sea necesario.
MAI-Code-1.1-Flash ya está disponible en GitHub Copilot, por lo que no necesitas descargar ni instalar nada. Para acceder a él se requiere una cuenta de GitHub con un plan de Copilot activo, ya sea individual o empresarial. Si cumples con este requisito, puedes usarlo dentro de VS Code o Visual Studio.

articles.title: The Charging Inlet Has Become a System: Rethinking EV Charge-Control Electronics - EE Times
articles.text:
The overlooked charge-control interface
Technical discussions of EV on-board chargers usually focus on the high-power conversion stage: SiC versus GaN, bidirectional topologies, power density, and high-voltage battery architectures. Those topics deserve attention, but they are not the only source of development risk. Engineers responsible for qualifying an on-board charger (OBC) also spend substantial effort on the low-voltage charge-control interface – the circuitry that monitors the Control Pilot (CP), Proximity Pilot (PP), and Protective Earth (PE) lines, detects connection and charging states, wakes the vehicle, and reports inlet status to the host controller.
On a block diagram, presented in Fig 1, this interface appears simple. In a production design, it is often distributed across comparators, op amps, precision dividers, DACs, level shifters, wake-up circuits, protection networks, and host-MCU firmware. Each element adds tolerance, failure modes, diagnostic requirements, qualification effort, and software dependencies.
That architecture was manageable when regional designs were largely independent and charging requirements were less consolidated. It is less attractive today. Global vehicle platforms must support multiple charging standards, and newer interfaces such as SAE J3400 and the Megawatt Charging System (MCS) increase expectations for measurement accuracy, robustness, interoperability, low standby current, and functional-safety support. The appropriate question is no longer whether the discrete implementation can be extended, but whether discrete analog plus MCU firmware remains the most efficient system architecture.
What the charge-control interface must do
Under IEC 61851-1, referred in Fig 2, the EV supply equipment (EVSE) generates a nominal 1 kHz CP waveform with positive and negative voltage excursions. The vehicle changes the positive CP level through its resistor-and-diode network: approximately +9 V indicates a connected vehicle, and approximately +6 V indicates that the vehicle is ready to accept energy. The negative half-cycle remains near -12 V and supports the diode-check function. The vehicle-side electronics must therefore detect the CP state levels and measure PWM duty cycle, which communicates the EVSE current limit. Because the signal is bipolar and exposed at the inlet, it cannot be connected directly to a typical MCU ADC; it requires protection, level translation, and accurately controlled thresholds.
The PP circuit identifies cable presence and, for applicable couplers, the cable assembly’s current capability through a resistor code. IEC 61851-1 values such as 1.5 kΩ, 680 Ω, 220 Ω, and 100 Ω correspond to 13 A, 20 A, 32 A, and 63 A cable ratings. The measurement path must distinguish these resistance ranges across component tolerance, temperature, connector aging, contamination, and contact resistance.
PE complicates the measurement reference. Protective Earth at the inlet may not be at exactly the same potential as the charge controller’s local ground or chassis reference, particularly during transients or when current flows in shared return paths. A design that interprets a PE-referenced pilot signal only against local ground can introduce systematic error. Robust implementations therefore account for the PE-to-local-ground offset, typically through PE-referenced or differential measurement capability.
When parked, the OBC and host MCU are normally in a low-power state, but the inlet must still detect a plug-in event, CP activity, or a relevant state change. This monitoring function is often allocated only tens of microamps from the 12 V battery. A discrete implementation usually requires ultra-low-power comparators, switchable bias networks, or an always-on MCU that periodically scans the inlet. The wake-up path consequently becomes a separate low-power subsystem with its own validation and fault analysis.
The engineering conclusion is straightforward: the charge-control interface is already a subsystem, even when its functions are distributed across many discrete components and firmware modules.
Why distributed monitoring is difficult
In a conventional electric-vehicle charge controller (EVCC), analog conditioning is implemented in discrete hardware, threshold decisions are split between comparators and firmware, PWM timing is captured by MCU peripherals, wake-up logic resides in an always-on power domain, and diagnostics are added around the available circuitry. The function is distributed across hardware and software boundaries rather than contained within a characterized measurement block.
This distribution creates three recurring engineering problems:
Tolerance accumulation: Divider ratios, amplifier offset, comparator thresholds, reference error, ADC gain, and temperature drift all contribute to the final measurement uncertainty. Demonstrating CP and PP accuracy across -40 °C to +125 °C can require a substantial worst-case analysis and calibration strategy.
Firmware coupling: The MCU does not merely consume a measurement; it often constructs the result by combining ADC samples, comparator flags, timer captures, debounce logic, and state-machine software. This coupling increases software complexity and expands the safety-related software scope.
Verification scope: Each boundary between conditioning, threshold detection, timing capture, wake-up logic, and diagnostics introduces another interaction to test. Verification must cover not only the individual blocks, but also their sequencing and fault behavior across voltage, temperature, and transient conditions.
One hardware platform, multiple charging standards
A global vehicle program may need to support CCS, SAE J3400/NACS, GB/T 18487, and, in selected markets or vehicle segments, CHAdeMO. These systems use related concepts – pilot signals, resistance coding, PWM, connection detection, and high-level communication – but differ in signal definitions, voltage ranges, connector topology, switch behavior, and charging sequences.
With a discrete architecture, those differences tend to become PCB differences: alternate divider networks, additional comparators, changed protection components, or separate regional schematics. Each derivative carries its own BOM, layout, manufacturing configuration, qualification evidence, software calibration, and field-debug history. This directly conflicts with the OEM objective of maintaining a common global electrical platform.
Automotive electronics has already followed this consolidation path in other domains. Functions once implemented with a discrete transceiver, watchdog, supervisor, nonvolatile memory, and diagnostic circuitry are now commonly integrated into system-basis devices. Charge-control electronics are subject to the same drivers: lower component count, fewer interfaces, defined diagnostic behavior, and easier platform reuse.
Why now: J3400 and MCS increase the requirements
Regional fragmentation alone might justify another incremental design cycle. The stronger argument for architectural change is that the measurement and safety requirements are increasing at the same time.
SAE J3400 standardizes NACS conductive charging and places greater emphasis on accurately interpreting inlet and connector states. For the PP path, this can require more than a coarse resistor classification; the controller may need an accurate resistance measurement with sufficient margin to distinguish closely spaced operating conditions and detect implausible states. In a vehicle safety concept, that measurement can also be assigned a high Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL), potentially up to ASIL D, based on the hazard analysis and risk assessment. The ASIL is therefore a vehicle-level allocation under ISO 26262, not a rating automatically conferred by the charging standard.
For a discrete implementation, a safety-related measurement path spans resistor networks, analog conditioning, comparators or ADCs, MCU peripherals, and software. The safety analysis must address drift, open and short faults, latent failures, dependent failures, timing faults, and diagnostic coverage across the complete chain. Redundant paths and plausibility checks can satisfy the safety goal, but they add components, calibration effort, and verification complexity.
MCS extends the same system pressure into megawatt-class commercial-vehicle charging. Its higher power levels, additional interoperability requirements, and demanding safety environment increase the value of a well-defined inlet-monitoring boundary. When a platform must already be requalified for a new charging interface, consolidating the low-voltage control architecture can be more efficient than continuing to add discrete functions to the legacy design.
An integrated charge-interface controller
One architectural alternative is a dedicated automotive IC positioned between the charging inlet and the host MCU. Rather than distributing the monitoring function across unrelated devices, the controller integrates the analog measurement, timing, wake-up, switching, and diagnostic functions behind a defined digital interface. A practical device in this class should provide:
High-voltage-tolerant analog front ends: CP, PP/CC/CC1/CC2, and PE inputs must tolerate the normal signal range, inlet transients, and specified fault conditions. The measurement architecture should support local-ground and PE-referenced measurements where required.
Shared precision measurement resources: Characterized ADC, DAC, and comparator resources can be routed to multiple inlet signals, replacing cascaded discrete chains. Accuracy, offset, temperature drift, and diagnostic limits are then specified at the IC boundary rather than inferred from individual component specifications.
Hardware CP timing measurement: Dedicated capture logic can measure CP frequency, high time, low time, and duty cycle without depending on software polling or interrupt latency. The host receives latched timing results for its charging-state algorithm.
Autonomous low-power monitoring: A low-power scan engine can periodically bias and sample selected inlet signals while the host is asleep. When programmable voltage, resistance, or timing conditions are met, the device can assert a wake or power-enable output and latch the event for later diagnosis. Duty-cycled biasing can reduce average parked current to the tens-of-microamps range.
Supervised control outputs: The IC can control standard-defined switches, such as the IEC 61851 S2 function, while monitoring command-versus-state consistency and placing outputs in a defined state after a detected fault.
Defined digital and fault interfaces: A serial interface should expose measurements, configuration, status, and diagnostic information, while dedicated interrupt and fault pins provide deterministic notification independent of normal software traffic.
The objective is not to integrate features for their own sake; it is to establish a characterized subsystem boundary and remove unnecessary interfaces. Fewer discrete stages reduce solder joints, tolerance contributors, supplier dependencies, PCB area, and manufacturing-test points. Integration does concentrate functionality in one IC, so the component must provide adequate diagnostics, fault containment, and a documented safe-state strategy. When those conditions are met, the reduction in system verification and safety-case effort can exceed the direct BOM savings.
From integrated hardware to a software-defined charging platform
Configurability turns integration from a component-cost decision into a platform decision. Software-defined vehicle architectures favor stable hardware whose behavior and regional variation are controlled through validated software and configuration data. A discrete EVCC works against that objective because many standard-specific choices are fixed by resistor values, routing, and component population.
A configurable charge-interface controller can support a common controller PCB across multiple charging standards, subject to the connector, protection, and power-path differences required by each region. Programmable thresholds, selectable measurement references, flexible signal routing, and configurable wake-up conditions move a larger portion of the regional behavior into initialization data rather than PCB variants. The resulting platform provides three practical advantages:
Unified controller hardware: A common measurement and control architecture reduces regional PCB derivatives, BOM variants, calibration procedures, and manufacturing configurations.
Controlled adaptability: Validated configuration sets can accommodate approved changes in thresholds, timing, wake-up criteria, and diagnostic behavior without redesigning the analog front end.
Cleaner software boundaries: The host MCU receives calibrated measurements, latched events, and diagnostic status rather than managing continuous analog sampling, comparator polling, and timer capture. Charging application software can therefore target a stable device abstraction instead of a board-specific analog implementation.
Silicon alone is not sufficient. The device must be supported by production-quality drivers, a portable API, configuration and calibration tools, reference schematics, and validated parameter sets for the targeted standards. These deliverables should be evaluated alongside the electrical specifications; without them, integration merely moves complexity from hardware into system software.
Integration can simplify the functional-safety case
Functional safety is where a distributed implementation creates the greatest engineering burden and where a well-designed integrated device can provide the most leverage.
In a discrete design, the Tier-1 or OEM must assemble the safety argument from component data supplied by multiple vendors: resistor-network failure modes, op-amp and comparator drift, MCU ADC and timer behavior, firmware diagnostics, and dependent-failure interactions. Passive-network faults can be difficult to diagnose, and every regional variant changes the evidence. The resulting safety case is highly system-specific.
An integrated device can simplify – not eliminate – that work by providing:
Built-in safety mechanisms: Reference and supply monitors, periodic self-tests, measurement-path plausibility checks, ADC or comparator diagnostics, and configuration-integrity checks can be designed with the protected functions and characterized by the IC supplier.
Defined fault semantics: Dedicated fault signaling, latched diagnostic registers, documented fault reaction times, and a defined safe state give the system architect a deterministic boundary for fault detection and response.
Safety documentation: A Safety Manual and supporting FMEDA or safety analysis can document assumptions of use, diagnostic coverage, residual failure rates, integration requirements, and constraints on the system-level safety concept.
The OEM remains responsible for the vehicle-level safety goal, ASIL allocation, decomposition, and confirmation measures. Integration is valuable because it replaces a loosely coupled chain of components with one characterized element whose failure behavior is documented. That makes the system safety analysis more tractable, but it does not make functional safety a component-only property.
What engineers should evaluate
Engineers evaluating this device class should examine the complete subsystem boundary. Key criteria include measurement accuracy specified across supply and temperature; input fault tolerance and transient robustness; PE-referenced or differential measurement capability; configurable support for the targeted charging standards; autonomous low-power monitoring with defined wake-up latency; hardware PWM timing capture; diagnostic coverage and fault reaction behavior; development as an ISO 26262 safety element out of context (SEooC), when required; an appropriate AEC-Q100 temperature grade and mission profile; and production-ready software, calibration, and configuration tools.
The concepts and architecture presented here are reflected in Lumissil’s IS32CG1112, an integrated EV charging-interface IC developed to support next-generation vehicle charge-control designs.
Conclusion
The OBC power stage will remain central to EV charging performance, but the low-voltage inlet interface has become a significant contributor to component count, software complexity, verification effort, and functional-safety workload. Replacing distributed analog conditioning and firmware-defined measurement with a configurable, safety-documented charge-interface controller can create a cleaner engineering boundary. Regional behavior can be implemented through validated configuration data, while measurement, wake-up, timing, and fault handling remain within a characterized subsystem. As J3400 and MCS enter more vehicle programs, this architecture offers a practical path toward a reusable global platform rather than another generation of regional patches.

articles.title: Whatsapp: So siehst du künftig empfangene Bilder und Videos, ohne deine Nachrichten zu öffnen
articles.text:
Whatsapp: So siehst du künftig empfangene Bilder und Videos, ohne deine Nachrichten zu öffnen
Wer viele Nachrichten in Messengern wie Whatsapp bekommt, wird gelegentlich den Überblick über Chats verlieren. Deshalb arbeitet Meta immer wieder daran, die Übersicht in der App zu verbessern. Erst kürzlich hat das Unternehmen Whatsapp drei Neuerungen verpasst, um Gruppenkonversationen zu verbessern. Jetzt folgt schon die nächste Verbesserung, die allerdings alle Chats betrifft.
So bringt Whatsapp mehr Überblick für Medien
Wie WABetaInfo berichtet, arbeitet Meta aktuell daran, dir mehr Informationen an die Hand zu geben, sobald dir einer deiner Kontakte einen Sticker, ein Bild oder ein Video sendet. Aktuell bekommst du dann in der Übersicht aller Chats nur den Hinweis angezeigt, welcher Medientyp dir zugesendet wurde. Haben dir mehrere Whatsapp-Kontakte parallel Videos oder Bilder geschickt, ist es auf den ersten Blick noch unmöglich, zu wissen, was sie zeigen.
Das soll sich mit einer kleinen, aber praktischen Neuerung ändern. Denn künftig zeigt dir Whatsapp neben der Information, dass es sich um einen Sticker, ein Foto oder ein Video handelt, auch ein kleines Vorschaubild davon an. In der aktuellen Version des Features können Fotos und Videos auch anhand des Vorschaubildes einfach voneinander unterschieden werden. Denn Videos bekommen noch einen kleinen Play-Button verpasst.
Die Whatsapp-Neuerung lohnt sich primär dann, wenn du nicht jede Nachricht mit einem Foto, Videos oder Stickern öffnen willst, um deren Inhalte zu sehen. So kannst du einfach einen Blick auf das Vorschaubild werfen und entscheiden, ob du die Konversation direkt aufrufen möchtest oder der Chat auch noch etwas warten kann.
Noch musst du dich auf das Whatsapp-Feature ein wenig gedulden. Zumindest dann, wenn du nicht Teil des Betaprogramms bist. Denn aktuell rollt Meta die Neuerung nur an User:innen aus, die an der Android-Beta teilnehmen. Sollte die Testphase ohne große Probleme ablaufen, könnte die Neuerung auch bald schon in der Release-Version von Whatsapp landen.

articles.title: Ferrari Luce à 40 millions de dollars : pourquoi cette enchère record ne dit rien du succès du modèle - Numerama
articles.text:
Les enchères de la maison RM Sotheby’s ont pris une tournure complètement inattendue avec le « Châssis 0 » de la Ferrari Luce. Le tout premier modèle 100 % électrique de Maranello, qui a été largement moqué à son lancement, se transforme subitement en star absolue de la Monterey Car Week 2026 en faisant s’envoler les enchères.
Le véhicule, estimé à un peu plus d’un million de dollars, a été adjugé le 16 août à 40 millions de dollars (environ 34,5 millions d’euros). Il établit un nouveau record écrasant le précédent, établi en 2025, pour la Ferrari Daytona SP3. Pourtant, penser que ce chiffre mirobolant reflète la désirabilité réelle de cette berline électrique à cinq places est une illusion.
Une enchère caritative n’est pas une enchère comme les autres
Le premier élément pour garder la tête froide réside dans la nature même de la vente : il s’agit d’une vente 100 % caritative au profit de la Ferrari Foundation, reconnue comme organisme de bienfaisance.
Pour l’acheteur américain, ces 40 millions de dollars ne représentent pas le « juste prix » d’une voiture, mais un don philanthropique massivement déductible de ses impôts. L’homme bien connu dans le milieu est d’ailleurs le philanthrope qui a déjà remporté les enchères de la Daytona SP3 l’an dernier avec un montant de 26 millions de dollars, comme le précise le journaliste Jean-Pierre Gagick sur ses réseaux sociaux. Nul doute qu’avec de tels dons, l’homme est en tête de liste pour l’acquisition des modèles les plus rares du constructeur.
Ce qu’il faut savoir, c’est que dans une vente aux enchères caritative, le montant payé au‑dessus de la valeur réelle du lot (et non pas simplement au‑dessus de la mise de départ) est fiscalement déductible comme don. Si l’on voulait grossir le trait, cet acheteur vient de s’offrir 39 millions de dollars de déduction fiscale, en plus du premier exemplaire de la Luce produit par Ferrari.
Le mythe du « sold out » des modèles 2026 vacille
Depuis la présentation houleuse de la Luce en mai dernier, Ferrari veut reprendre la main sur le narratif autour du modèle. Le constructeur maîtrise sa communication d’une main de fer en essayant de renverser la vapeur en sa faveur.
La marque affirme ainsi que les ventes se portent mieux que prévu et répète depuis à l’envi que tout le quota d’immatriculations prévu pour 2026 est d’ores et déjà réservé. Il est bien sûr impossible de vérifier ces informations. D’ailleurs, on ne sait même pas combien de véhicules représente ce quota : quelques dizaines, centaines ou milliers d’exemplaires ? Ferrari n’a pas souhaité s’exprimer sur ce point.
Des témoignages circulant chez certains clients européens suggèrent toutefois que des créneaux de production pour 2026 seraient encore proposés. Impossible, à ce stade, de vérifier l’ampleur réelle du phénomène. Néanmoins, les chiffres d’immatriculations finiront de toute façon par révéler la vérité d’ici la fin de l’année, que ce soit en Europe ou en Chine.
En attendant, une voiture de série vendue plus de soixante fois son prix catalogue dans le cadre d’un gala de charité ne transforme pas cette nouveauté électrique contestée en icône instantanée. Cela prouve simplement qu’un milliardaire a trouvé un moyen spectaculaire d’allier philanthropie, optimisation fiscale et relations publiques auprès de la marque au cheval cabré. Le débat sur la pertinence et la désirabilité de la Ferrari Luce, lui, reste entier. De notre côté, on reste sur la réserve et on attend de voir l’arrivée du modèle sur le marché dans les prochains mois pour faire un éventuel mea culpa à Ferrari.

articles.title: Une faille Windows permet de désactiver l'antivirus avec un simple script
articles.text:
Des chercheurs ont présenté une méthode capable de neutraliser l’antivirus et les protections noyau de Windows avec un seul script. Microsoft a corrigé la faille sous-jacente, CVE-2026-23670, dès avril, mais des millions de barrettes de mémoire vendues sans protection en écriture restent exploitables.
« Download More RAM » s’en prend aux puces de configuration des barrettes DDR4 et DDR5, qui indiquent à la carte mère la quantité de mémoire installée. En les reprogrammant par logiciel, un attaquant fait croire à l’ordinateur qu’il dispose de deux fois plus de mémoire que la réalité. Les adresses fictives se superposent alors aux adresses réelles.
Les chercheurs appellent ce phénomène l’aliasing mémoire. Il permet de lire et de modifier des zones que Windows protège habituellement même contre un utilisateur disposant des droits administrateur, via deux remparts : la sécurité basée sur la virtualisation (VBS) et l’intégrité de code appliquée par l’hyperviseur (HVCI).
Le script qui coupe l’antivirus rétablit aussi des pilotes bannis
« Notre travail exploite le fait que tous les processus partagent la même mémoire pour contourner les garanties de sécurité les plus fortes de Windows », explique le professeur Tom Chothia, de l’université de Birmingham. « Les attaques précédentes de ce type nécessitaient un tournevis et un accès physique à la machine. Celle-ci n'a besoin que d'un script ». Le maître de conférences Marius Muench précise : « Windows fait une promesse forte : même un attaquant disposant des droits administrateur ne peut pas toucher au noyau sécurisé. Nous avons découvert que cette promesse repose sur l'hypothèse que la mémoire dit vrai sur sa propre taille. Sur une bonne partie de la mémoire que les gens achètent réellement, ce n'est pas le cas ».
Trois fabricants très présents chez les joueurs, Corsair, G.Skill et ADATA, vendent des barrettes totalement dépourvues de cette protection en écriture : ensemble, ils représentent 55 % du marché de la mémoire haute performance et plus de 70 % du segment gaming, selon l’université de Birmingham. Crucial, Kingston, HyperX et une partie de la gamme G.Skill offrent une protection partielle, suffisante pour bloquer l'’attaque.
Une fois la protection mémoire contournée, les chercheurs ont enchaîné plusieurs scénarios dans un seul script. Le plus direct coupe l’antivirus et les outils de détection et réponse (EDR). Le même accès permet aussi de réactiver des pilotes signés mais bannis pour leurs failles connues, de contourner le verrouillage de gestion des appareils en entreprise, ou de désactiver les protections anti-triche des jeux vidéo qui s’exécutent au niveau du noyau. C’est justement HVCI qui est censé bloquer automatiquement ces pilotes vulnérables une fois recensés : en rendant la mémoire menteuse sur sa propre taille, l’attaque prive Windows de ce filet de sécurité avant qu’il ne puisse agir.
Un correctif publié quatre mois avant la présentation publique
Microsoft a intégré un correctif pour CVE-2026-23670 dans sa mise à jour de sécurité d’avril, plusieurs mois avant que les chercheurs ne présentent leurs travaux à USENIX. Le Secure Boot, activé par défaut sur la plupart des PC vendus depuis 2022, bloque également l’attaque. Sur les systèmes équipés de mémoire non protégée, deux outils permettent de verrouiller rétroactivement les puces de configuration : iCue, chez Corsair, et HWinfo, gratuit et compatible avec plusieurs marques. Certaines cartes mères proposent aussi, dans leur BIOS, une option pour bloquer l’écriture sur ces puces.
L'’étude, intitulée « Download More RAM: Dismantling Windows Operating System Defences with Mischievous Memory » et menée avec Sam Collins, William Burgess et David Oswald, a reçu le Distinguished Paper Award du symposium USENIX Security 2026.

articles.title: Efficiency, lifespan, environment: test your business creativity with Edition 245 of our weekly quiz!
articles.text:
Efficiency, lifespan, environment: test your business creativity with Edition 245 of our weekly quiz!
This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 245th quiz. Ready?
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 245th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.
What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?
Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.
Q1: Recycling glass
The glass recycling chain involves an informal community of collectors and aggregators, but does not have accurate sourcing data. How can this gap be met so that brands can show they have met recycling targets?
Q2: Age and lifestyle
Many people give up active lifestyles once they turn 60, and are dismissed as ‘senior citizens’. How can they be effectively supported to carry on physical, mental and social activities?
Q3: Satellite lifespan
Many geostationary satellites have generated enormous revenues but are retired simply because they run out of fuel. Where is the entrepreneurial opportunity here?
Q4: EV efficiency
EV drivers who earn by the trip lose money every minute they spend on charging instead of driving. How can efficiency and run time be improved here?
Q5: Lending for growth
Traditional lending to MSMEs often relies heavily on collateral and rigid historical data, leaving out many companies who may be credit-worthy. How can this gap be tackled?
Answers!
Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!
A1: Recycling glass
Founded by Iwan Richard, Karthik Sankar, Varun Pandithurai and Mohammad Mohiyeddin, Reneonix is building circular materials infrastructure for the packaging industry. It covers collection, sorting, processing, logistics, and reporting for a brand or manufacturer.
It returns both the glass material and the paperwork that goes with it. Read more here about its AI-led sorting of incoming glass, traceability framework, and conversion methods to create specification-grade raw material.
A2: Age and lifestyle
Founded by Deval Delivala and Ashwini Kapila, WalkAbout India is a dedicated community platform for active adults aged 55 and above. ““All our experiences cater to learning, finding purpose, and helping older adults live a better life,” Delivala says.
It offers reskilling classes to teach active agers how to create impact in life, and runs an accelerator programme for those who want to start a business venture. Read more here about how it also helps people pursue their hobbies via classes in music, dance, poetry writing, art, and craft.
A3: Satellite lifespan
Founded by Jay Panchal, Nithyaa Giri, and Hrishit Tambi, Aule Space helps satellite operators extend operational life of existing satellites and avoid launching entirely new satellites. Its ‘jetpack satellite’ is a spacecraft that docks with the satellite and provides propulsion.
The on-orbit satellite servicing market is projected to reach about $5.5 billion by 2030. Read more here about how Aule eventually plans to get into extraterrestrial robotics and then asteroid mining by 2050.
A4: EV efficiency
Founded by Sanskar Modi, SunCharge Motors puts solar panels on three-wheeler EVs so that they generate part of the energy needed right while they are being driven. It helps address some of the challenges in finding accessible charging infrastructure and reliable power supply.
The product is designed for commercial fleets, whose economics rest on hours worked per day rather than on purchase price alone. Read more here about the startup’s battery management system and real-time energy controls, and its recent fundraise led by the JITO Incubation and Innovation Foundation.
A5: Lending for growth
Founded by Bhavik Vasa, GetVantage is a B2B fintech platform for MSMEs that offers a full suite of cash-flow-based financing, term loans, business loans, and merchant cash advances. It is specifically tailored to small businesses’ operating cycles.
“The next decade of India's growth relies on unlocking credit for millions of MSMEs,” observes investor Rajeev Ahuja, former MD of RBL Bank. Read more here about the startup’s API capabilities that enable B2B ecommerce platforms embed financing options directly into their merchant ecosystems.
YourStory has also published the pocketbook ‘Proverbs and Quotes for Entrepreneurs: A World of Inspiration for Startups’ as a creative and motivational guide for innovators.

Deux pliants ultra-fins, mais pas aussi rassurants
Ouverts, les deux ressemblent à de petites tablettes : 4,1 mm d’épaisseur pour le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, 4 mm pour le Magic V6. Le modèle de Samsung est toutefois plus léger avec 215 g contre 224 g. Sa charnière paraît solide, sa pliure est très discrète et son châssis mêle aluminium, verre renforcé et titane. Son bloc photo le fait en revanche trembler sur une table.
Le nouveau pliant de Honor est plus stable et surtout mieux protégé. Sa certification IP68/69 couvre poussière, immersion et jets d’eau, loin devant l’IP48 du Fold 8 Ultra. La firme chinois le rend également compatible avec un stylet vendu séparément, alors que Samsung abandonne le S Pen. Tous deux proposent 5G, NFC, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 et lecteur d’empreintes latéral.
Samsung éblouit, Honor affiche des couleurs plus justes
Côté affichage, tous deux utilisent des écrans Amoled LTPO (jusqu’à 120 Hz. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra dispose d’un cover display de 6,5 pouces et 8 pouces à l’intérieur ; le Magic V6, 6,52 et 7,95 pouces. Le sud-coréen domine nettement en luminosité avec environ 2880 cd/m² sur ses deux dalles, contre 2043 cd/m² à l’extérieur et 1325 cd/m² à l’intérieur chez Honor.
Le V6 se rattrape avec un antireflet remarquable et des couleurs presque parfaites une fois le bon mode activé. Samsung reste excellent en plein soleil et réduit lui aussi fortement les reflets sur son grand écran, mais son réglage le plus fidèle réchauffe un peu trop l’image.
Même puissance, énorme différence de température
Nos deux duellistes embarquent une puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 et font tourner sans peine plusieurs apps en même temps ou des jeux exigeants. La vraie différence apparaît avec la chaleur : le modèle de Samsung reste autour de 42°C sous forte charge, quand le pliant signé Honor a atteint 54°C avant de se mettre en sécurité.
Côté logiciel, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra tourne sous Android 17 avec One UI 9, et bénéficie de sept ans de support logiciel. Le Magic V6 reste sous Android 16, avec sept ans de mises à jour également, beaucoup d’outils d’IA et une prise en charge des AirPods, AirDrop et des notifications Apple. Il arrive cependant avec trop d’applications préinstallées.
Photo et autonomie : Honor sort les gros chiffres
Samsung réunit un capteur principal de 200 Mpx, un ultra grand-angle de 50 Mpx et un zoom optique x3 de 10 Mpx. De jour, ses photos sont détaillées, naturelles et bien exposées. L’ultra grand-angle convainc aussi, mais le zoom perd beaucoup de précision la nuit. Les deux caméras selfie de 10 Mpx sont correctes et la vidéo monte jusqu’en 8K à 30 i/s.
Honor joue davantage la régularité avec 50 Mpx pour le module principal et l’ultra grand-angle, puis 64 Mpx pour le zoom x3. Les couleurs sont plus vives et son téléobjectif conserve davantage de détails dans l’obscurité. Les deux capteurs selfie atteignent 20 Mpx et la vidéo arrière culmine en 4K 60 i/s.
Samsung adopte enfin le silicium-carbone pour sa batterie de 5000 mAh : 21 h 27 min d’autonomie moyenne et 56 min pour une charge complète à 45 W. Honor propose une capacité encore plus généreuse de 6660 mAh et tient en moyenne 22 h 21 min. Le V6 supporte une charge 80 W en filaire et 66 W sans-fil, mais demande tout de même 1 h 24 min pour faire le plein.
On fait le bilan, calmement
Ces deux smartphones pliants haut de gamme méritent amplement leurs 5 étoiles. Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra est le plus équilibré : plus léger, beaucoup plus lumineux, particulièrement à l’aise en multitâche et peu sujet aux montées de fièvre. Son étanchéité limitée, l’absence de stylet et ses photos de nuit au téléobjectif restent cependant ses principales faiblesses.
Le Honor Magic V6, lui, met le paquet sur l’équipement avec sa batterie XXL, sa protection IP68/69, et la constance de son volet photo. En revanche, sa chauffe importante sous forte sollicitation est son vrai point noir. À prix voisin, Samsung privilégie donc le confort et la maîtrise, tandis que Honor mise sur l’autonomie et l’équipement. Vous voilà prévenus.

articles.title: Google ouvre le Play Store à la concurrence, mais fait tout pour dissuader les utilisateurs d’aller voir ailleurs
articles.text:
Aux États-Unis, le Play Store s’est officiellement ouvert à la concurrence. Cependant, télécharger un magasin d’applications tiers relève du parcours du combattant. Entre un écran d’avertissement, une boîte de dialogue ou encore des demandes de confirmation, tout est fait pour décourager les utilisateurs. Un juge américain a ordonné à Google de mettre un terme à ces pratiques jugées anticoncurrentielles. L’Europe pourrait s’en inspirer.
Google ouvre le Play Store à la concurrence
Nous vous en parlions en mars dernier, après avoir perdu son procès contre Epic Games, Google a annoncé plusieurs changements au niveau du mode de fonctionnement du Play Store. L’entreprise de Mountain View a notamment ouvert son magasin d’applications aux services de paiement tiers, ainsi qu’aux boutiques tierces d’applications. Pour l’instant, aux États-Unis, un seul magasin d’applications tiers est disponible sur le Play Store, à savoir Aptoide.
Sur le Play Store américain, il est donc dorénavant possible de télécharger plus facilement des magasins d’applications tiers. Du moins, en théorie. Dans les faits, Google mobilise différents moyens pour décourager ceux qui seraient tentés d’aller voir ailleurs. Un juge américain vient d’ailleurs de rappeler Google à l’ordre.
Une ouverture à la concurrence parsemée d’obstacles
Le moins que l’on puisse dire, c’est que télécharger un magasin d’applications tiers sur le Play Store américain n’est pas très fluide. Avant d’accéder au bouton permettant le téléchargement, l’utilisateur fait face à un bouton « Afficher le contenu », à des demandes de confirmation, à une boîte de dialogue comportant plusieurs étapes ou encore à un écran d’avertissement stipulant que Google n’a pas contrôlé le store en question. En d’autres termes, Google a ouvert son Play Store à la concurrence, tout en instaurant plusieurs étapes visant à dissuader les utilisateurs du Play Store d’aller chez la concurrence.
Justement, un juge américain a qualifié ces contraintes de « frictions anticoncurrentielles » et a demandé à Google de les supprimer dans un délai d’une semaine. Un magasin d’applications tiers devra ainsi être téléchargeable aussi facilement que n’importe quelle application Android. De son côté, Google affirme que ces contraintes ont été instaurées afin d’assurer la sécurité de ses utilisateurs. Le tribunal a estimé qu’un argument de sécurité ne peut pas servir de prétexte pour maintenir une position dominante sur le marché.
Enfin, rappelons que l’ouverture totale du Play Store à la concurrence, ainsi que l’obligation pour Google de simplifier le processus de téléchargement, concernent uniquement les États-Unis. Néanmoins, le Digital Markets Act (DMA) pourrait pousser l’entreprise de Mountain View à suivre le même chemin sur le Vieux Continent.

articles.title: Tras 20 años sin poner en marcha un aerogenerador nuevo, Euskadi comienza las obras de un parque eólico en Labraza
articles.text:
El País Vasco no ponía en marcha un aerogenerador nuevo desde 2006. Ahora lo va a hacer con el proyecto de Labraza, con más de 50 millones de inversión inicial y una presencia notable de la cadena de suministro local en su construcción.
Un proyecto estratégico. El pasado mes de noviembre se iniciaron las obras del nuevo parque eólico en Labraza, municipio de Oion. Según los datos del ejecutivo regional, el proyecto cuenta con una inversión de 56 millones de euros y la gestión de Aixeindar, una sociedad de colaboración público-privada creada por Iberdrola y el Ente Vasco de la Energía del Gobierno Vasco. Una vez en funcionamiento, la previsión es de una potencia de 40 megavatios, gracias a ocho aerogeneradores del modelo SG 5.0-145 (2.0) de cinco megavatios cada uno, pertenecientes a la plataforma 4X.
Con esta nueva instalación, la potencia eólica instalada de Euskadi aumentará de los actuales 155 megavatios a 193, en un incremento del 26%, y dará energía renovable a más de 30.000 hogares. Además, ahorrará en emisiones de gases a la atmósfera 16.300 toneladas de CO2, según el gobierno.
De hecho, tal es su importancia que el Departamento de Equilibrio Territorial y Ordenación del Territorio de la Diputación Foral de Álava lo ha declarado de interés público.
Todo queda en casa. Uno de los aspectos más reseñables de este nuevo proyecto es que la fabricación de las piezas necesarias para este parque supondrá un importante impulso a la cadena de suministro vasca, como apunta El Español.
Por un lado, las obras se han adjudicado a la firma navarra Ecay Construcciones; por otro, las multiplicadoras se confeccionarán en las instalaciones de Asteasu, en Gipuzkoa y la subestación irá a manos de EDS Ingeniería y Montaje, en Galdakao, Bizkaia. Y por último, los ocho aerogeneradores correrán a cargo de Siemens Gamesa, que, por primera vez en varios años está registrando ganancias, por un valor de más de 50 millones de euros.
Un traslado pionero. Estos días se está produciendo la llegada de las primeras palas de los aerogeneradores. Como explican desde Navarra Capital, con frecuencia, el transporte de este tipo de infraestructuras suele suponer todo un reto logístico, ya que al enorme tamaño de los componentes de los aerogeneradores se le suele sumar, además, la localización remota de los proyectos para conseguir buenas cantidades de recurso eólico. En este caso, de hecho, el principal obstáculo orográfico que presenta Labraza son las curvas angostas desde Campezo, con un trazado extremadamente sinuoso debido a las montañas.
Para salvarlo, se ha empleado la tecnología Blade Lifter, que emplea la inclinación que ya tiene la pala para facilitar su transporte, utilizando un elevador hidráulico que se coloca justo detrás de la cabeza tractora de la grúa que la lleva. Gracias a este mecanismo, la pala puede inclinarse en mayor o menor ángulo o girar, según las necesidades de cada momento. Así, es posible transportarla por carreteras estrechas, curvas cerradas o, incluso, núcleos urbanos donde el espacio es más limitado.
Además, esta innovación reduce el impacto medioambiental que normalmente tienen este tipo de construcciones, ya que de esta manera se evita el trabajo de tener que modificar el trazado de carreteras.
Buscando el beneficio local. La construcción de este parque, según la web del Gobierno Vasco, creará unos 90 empleos que serán fundamentalmente locales. Las previsiones también apuntan a que supondrá un ingreso inicial para las arcas municipales de 1,2 millones de euros y unos ingresos recurrentes de más de 200.000 euros al año.
Además, se puso en marcha un crowdlending para que la población local pudiera participar en la financiación del parque que ha conseguido más del doble de solicitudes disponibles: en total, la demanda real ha superado los seis millones de euros frente a los tres millones ofertados en un principio, según los datos que comparte el ejecutivo.
