articles.title: World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers
articles.text:
World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers
Scientists have built a tiny superconducting heat engine that turns quantum-scale heat into useful work—and could help make massive quantum computers far easier to build.
- Date:
- August 14, 2026
- Source:
- Aalto University
- Summary:
- A tiny superconducting engine has successfully converted heat near absolute zero into useful work, demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine of its kind. Future versions could operate autonomously inside quantum computers, potentially eliminating huge numbers of costly, noise-producing microwave cables.
- Share:
A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.
The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?
A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World
Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.
The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.
Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an important objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.
The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.
Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero
To make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.
"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.
The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.
"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.
Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.
"This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.
Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware
The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.
That capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.
"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.
Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.
The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Aalto University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tuomas Uusnäkki, Timm Mörstedt, Wallace Teixeira, Miika Rasola, Mikko Möttönen. Initial demonstration of a quantum heat engine based on dissipation-engineered superconducting circuits. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-72651-x

articles.title: Ces nouveaux satellites pourraient bouleverser le ciel au nom de l’énergie solaire
articles.text:
Les satellites équipés de miroirs s’annoncent comme l’une des solutions aux limites actuelles des énergies renouvelables. Placés en orbite, ces miroirs spatiaux peuvent réfléchir la lumière du Soleil vers la Terre lorsque celle-ci est plongée dans l’obscurité. Sur Terre, des centrales solaires utilisent ce faisceau lumineux pour produire de l’électricité, même la nuit. Si la promesse a de quoi donner de l’espoir, plusieurs experts alertent sur les risques qu’une telle technologie pourrait engendrer. En effet, les miroirs de ces satellites réfléchissent vers la Terre un faisceau lumineux susceptible d’avoir un impact majeur sur l’astronomie, les êtres humains et la nature.
Des miroirs dans l’espace pour produire de l’énergie solaire la nuit
Amazon compte déployer plus de 8 000 satellites dans le ciel au cours de ces prochaines années. De son côté, Starlink en dispose déjà de plus de 10 000 et se félicite régulièrement de nouveaux déploiements réussis. Il s’agit là de deux exemples qui permettent de comprendre la course au déploiement des satellites. Mais cela n’est pas tout. À cela s’ajoute maintenant l’arrivée des satellites équipés de miroirs réfléchissant la lumière du Soleil vers la Terre. Ceux-ci promettent une énergie renouvelable 24 heures sur 24, 7 jours sur 7.
À titre d’exemple, l’entreprise californienne Reflect Orbital compte lancer un satellite équipé d’un miroir spatial de 18 m², capable de fournir de l’énergie solaire à la demande. L’entreprise a déjà reçu le feu vert de la Federal Communications Commission (FCC) et a pour objectif d’en envoyer 50 000 d’ici 2035. Une promesse donc d’une énergie renouvelable à la demande, mais qui s’accompagne de sérieuses craintes de la part d’experts.
Des impacts majeurs sur l’astronomie, les êtres humains et la nature ?
Selon certaines estimations, le miroir spatial conçu par Reflect Orbital pourrait être aussi brillant que Vénus depuis l’extérieur du faisceau et quatre fois plus brillant que la Lune à l’intérieur de celui-ci. Une telle luminosité pourrait avoir de multiples conséquences. Tout d’abord, elle pourrait perturber fortement l’astronomie. Selon Roohi Dalal, directrice adjointe chargée des politiques publiques de l’American Astronomical Society (AAS), le projet de 50 000 satellites-miroirs de Reflect Orbital « pourrait bien signer la fin de l’astronomie optique au sol ».
Ensuite, certains experts alertent sur les dangers de telles technologies pour les humains. Un astronome amateur pourrait subir des lésions oculaires permanentes s’il observe accidentellement le faisceau lumineux du satellite à travers son télescope. Justement, Reflect Orbital assure que la zone éclairée par son satellite couvrirait 24 km², mais certains experts estiment qu’elle sera bien plus large.
Enfin, et non des moindres, les satellites équipés de miroirs spatiaux risquent d’avoir un impact significatif sur les écosystèmes et les espèces migratrices. De façon plus générale, ces satellites-miroir risquent de contribuer à la pollution du ciel, qui est déjà à un stade avancé. Selon la Royal Astronomical Society, la lumière réfléchie par le satellite de Reflect Orbital pourrait rendre « le ciel nocturne trois à quatre fois plus lumineux » dans les zones concernées.
Roohi Dalal explique à ce propos : « Ce qui me rend triste, c’est que la plupart des gens n’ont probablement jamais vu la Voie lactée dans le ciel nocturne, ni un véritable ciel étoilé. Pour moi, c’était l’une des plus belles expériences de ma vie : pouvoir me rendre dans un endroit préservé de la pollution lumineuse et observer la Voie lactée. Sans avoir vécu cela, lorsqu’on vit dans des villes où la pollution lumineuse est si courante, il est difficile de comprendre ce que nous sommes en train de perdre et ce dont nous sommes privés ». À défaut de voir le ciel, nous bénéficierions donc d’une énergie renouvelable.

articles.title: New AmnesiaStealer macOS malware hijacks browser sessions via remote control
articles.text:
A new information-stealing malware called AmnesiaStealer, which targets macOS users via ClickFix attacks, includes a streaming module that allows the attacker to interactively control the victim's web browser.
A notable capability is copying the victim's Chromium profile, including its authentication state, and loading it into a hidden, headless browser on the infected system.
This allows the hacker to access victims' authenticated sessions while preserving the identifiers associated with the browser, host, and network.
AmnesiaStealer can collect data in 16 Chromium-based web browsers as well as other sensitive information, such as passwords, cryptocurrency wallets, Apple Notes and documents, and keychain data.
The malware is currently distributed through ClickFix campaigns that use a fake GitHub download page to drop a password-protected ZIP archive.
Researchers at Jamf, an Apple device management and security company, analyzed AmnesiaStealer's distribution and found that it used the same template previously used to spread the Atomic and MacSync infostealers.
The ClickFix command executes a shell-script loader that downloads and launches the password-protected archive containing the AmnesiaStealer Mach-O payload.
The malware captures the victim’s macOS password and uses it to collect keychain data, as well as browser profiles, Apple Notes, Telegram sessions, documents, system information, and cryptocurrency wallet data.
The researchers highlight that the malware features a component called stream_module, retrieved using the remote_stream command, which gives the malicious operator remote control over authenticated sessions deployed from a headless browser instance.
According to Jamf, AmnesiaStealer's stream_module can duplicate user profiles in seven Chromium-based browsers, including Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Vivaldi, Arc, Opera, Brave, and Chromium, because they share the same DevTools Protocol, launch flags, and cookie encryption.
The module launches the legitimate browser executable in headless mode with command-line switches that weaken browser defenses, duplicates the victim’s profile, and specifies its location for storing the profile data.
The malware then establishes a WebSocket channel that connects to the operator's relay and sends a JSON registration message containing the browser name and build.
The operator can then send commands over this channel, such as navigation and mouse clicks, while the malware returns status and tab information as JSON and transmits screencast frames as binary WebSocket messages.
A second WebSocket channel connects to the local headless Chromium instance through the browser’s webSocketDebuggerUrl, providing access to the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).
This allows the hacker to navigate websites with mouse and keyboard control, export or import cookies, and operate online portals using the victim’s existing authenticated sessions.
“The operator receives a live screencast of the session at around 3fps and can drive it with a full input set: keyboard, mouse, scroll, navigation and tab management,” Jamf explains.
"In effect the remote_stream command turns an infected host into a live, operator-driven browser running the victim's authenticated sessions, which is a materially different level of access from file collection."
According to the researchers, the AmnesiaStealer can exfiltrate cookies, saved logins, browsing history, bookmarks, extensions, local state, and other profile data from the 16 Chromium-based browsers it targets.
It also steals cryptocurrency wallet details and identifies them by enumerating extensions and IndexedDB data.
Jamf notes that the malware contains a fallback mechanism when it runs on macOS 26 and cannot recover the existing Chrome Safe Storage key, which replaced it with an attacker-supplied value.
This makes previously stored cookies and passwords permanently unreadable while allowing the attacker to decrypt data later.
The Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) has been abused by malware in the past, including by Chaos ransomware to hide command-and-control communications, and by Chaes malware to expose browser functions that could enable data theft.
However, AmnesiaStealer appears to be the first documented macOS malware to combine a cloned Chromium profile with CDP-based, live remote control, allowing attackers to interact with authenticated sessions through a hidden browser running on the infected computer.

articles.title: Acer Swift Air 14 : le rival du MacBook Neo est déjà 100 euros moins cher chez Boulanger
articles.text:
En mars 2026, Apple a lancé le MacBook Neo à 699 euros et a bousculé tout l’écosystème Windows. Depuis, les constructeurs travaillent sur une riposte, dans un contexte particulièrement difficile et Apple a dû augmenter le prix du MacBook.
Le Computex de juin a été l’occasion, pour les grandes marques, de présenter leurs rivaux : des portables légers avec un prix plus agressif, sous la barre des 900 euros. Nous avions alors découvert l’Acer Swift Air 14.
Vous vouliez un ordinateur portable d’exception ? Les PC équipés de Snapdragon tiennent leurs promesses.
Un PC qui va à l’essentiel
Châssis en aluminium de 1,19 kg pour 12,9 mm d’épaisseur, écran mat de 14 pouces en définition WUXGA (1920 x 1200) rafraîchi à 120 Hz, et une autonomie annoncée jusqu’à 19 heures en lecture vidéo, le Swift Air 14 mise sur la sobriété.
À l’intérieur, Acer inaugure les nouveaux processeurs Intel Core Series 3, des puces à six cœurs qui misent sur l’efficacité énergétique plutôt que sur la puissance brute. Elles devraient être suffisantes pour les mêmes tâches que le MacBook Neo : la bureautique, du web et de la visio.
899 euros sur l’étiquette, 699 dans le panier
Le prix conseillé du Swift Air 14 est de 899 euros, soit 100 euros de plus que le MacBook Neo, passé à 799 euros depuis la hausse de prix. Sur le papier, l’Acer est donc plus cher. Sauf que chez Boulanger, la version Intel Core Series 5 avec 8 Go de mémoire et 512 Go de stockage tombe à 699 euros.
L’ultraportable Windows passe alors sous le MacBook Neo, avec deux fois plus de stockage que la version d’Apple à 799 euros, limitée à 256 Go.
Face au MacBook Neo, chacun ses arguments
Sur la fiche technique, les deux machines se répondent presque point par point. Dans notre prise en main, nous avions souligné que l’écran 120 Hz du Swift Air 14 rend la navigation plus fluide que la dalle 60 Hz du MacBook Neo, et que sa caméra déverrouille le PC par reconnaissance faciale via Windows Hello, une option absente du Mac. L’écran de l’Acer plafonne à une définition 1080p, là où celui du Neo, plus défini, paraît plus net à l’œil.
Reste la plus grande différence, un PC sous Windows 11 d’un côté avec un processeur Intel x86, et un MacBook sous macOS avec une puce Apple Silicon de l’autre.

articles.title: What will the Moneris sale cost Canada?
articles.text:
Canadian payments processor Moneris, co-owned by banks RBC and BMO, announced its sale to a US private equity firm this week. If the $2-billion CAD deal is closed and approved, roughly one in three Canadian payments will run through a US-controlled entity.
Payment processing is an invisible but critical piece of economic infrastructure. With Moneris gone, Canada’s Big Five banks will soon mainly rely on US providers. As Vass Bednar of the Canadian Shield Institute pointed out, that means a foreign player will have “effective control over how the country’s commerce clears.”
Domestic tech solutions could help. Calgary’s Helcim is positioning itself to fill the vacuum left by Moneris. Its CEO, Nicolas Beique, told BetaKit that Helcim has seen a 30-percent jump in inbound calls this week from Canadian leads who want to support Canadian companies. Meanwhile, some have questioned whether Moneris itself is a valuable enough asset to worry about; a single payment processor isn’t necessarily as critical to sovereignty as the rails those payments run on.
But real-time rails aren’t here yet, and Moneris’s new ownership still creates a vulnerability. The long-awaited instant payment settlement is still on the way. It’s supposed to finally roll out in Q4 of this year, bringing faster and cheaper payments.
If nothing else, the Moneris sale could be a wake-up call for Canada to create the thriving payment ecosystem it has promised companies and consumers. A first step would be finally delivering sovereign payment rails and ensuring they can’t be bought.

articles.title: Leben wir in einer Simulation? Was Quantenphysik über unsere Realität verrät
articles.text:
Matrix oder Realität? Was hinter der Simulationstheorie steckt
Die Geschichte beginnt mit einem Missverständnis. Angeblich ist der Philosoph Nick Bostrom für die ganze Sache verantwortlich: Er soll 2003 einen Artikel veröffentlicht haben, in dem er nachweist, dass wir alle in einem Computerspiel leben. Gewissermaßen die akademische Begleitmusik zum Film Matrix, der 1999 in die Kinos kam.
Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?
Zwar hat Bostrom das genau genommen gar nicht getan – die Geschichte ist ein bisschen komplizierter –, doch Bostroms Vorstoß hat eine wissenschaftliche Debatte losgetreten, die fundamentale philosophische Fragen genauso berührt wie Erkenntnisse aus der Informatik, der Mathematik, der Kognitionsforschung, der Kosmologie und der theoretischen Physik. So gesehen ist es wenig überraschend, dass der wissenschaftliche Streit noch immer nicht beigelegt ist. Möglicherweise könnten physikalische Experimente die Frage, ob wir in einer Simulation leben, klären. Nur scheinen die Forschenden, die sich mit diesen Experimenten befassen, im Zuge ihrer Forschungen selbst in eine Zwischenwelt aus Annahmen, Definitionen und komplexer Mathematik zu gleiten.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 5/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit der Komplexität von Modellen in der Biologie, der Umwelt und der Gesellschaft – und wie KI diese simulierten Welten vorantreibt. Das Heft könnt ihr ab sofort online bestellen und im Zeitschriftenhandel erwerben..
Zurück zum Anfang: Nick Bostrom, der 2003 in der Fachzeitschrift Philosophical Quarterly ein Paper mit dem suggestiven Titel Are You Living in a Computer Simulation? veröffentlichte, ist nicht irgendein beliebiger Philosoph. Bostrom ist überzeugter Transhumanist und damit einerseits der festen Meinung, dass die Menschheit mithilfe von Technologie eine höhere Entwicklungsstufe erreichen kann. Andererseits befürchten Transhumanisten, dass sich die menschliche Zivilisation auf dem Weg dorthin mithilfe eben dieser fortschrittlicheren Technologien vorher selbst ins Aus schießt. 2002 prägt Bostrom in einem Aufsatz dafür den Begriff „existential risks“ – existenzielle Risiken. Etwa seit dieser Zeit forscht er an der Wahrscheinlichkeit für verschiedene dieser Risiken.
Nick Bostrom gibt drei Antworten auf die Frage, ob wir in einer Simulation leben
Bostrom fragt zwar, ob wir in einer Simulation leben, behauptet es jedoch tatsächlich nicht. Stattdessen gebe es drei verschiedene Antworten auf diese Frage, die einander ausschlössen. Welche davon richtig sei, so Bostrom, könnten wir schlicht nicht entscheiden.
Die erste: Die Menschheit stirbt aus, bevor sie die technischen Möglichkeiten einer „posthumanen“ Zivilisation erreicht hat. Zweitens könnte es Zivilisationen im Universum geben, die dieses technische Level erreicht haben, aber kein Interesse daran haben, eine simulierte Welt zu erschaffen. Oder wir leben drittens tatsächlich in einer Simulation. „In dem dunklen Wald unserer gegenwärtigen Unwissenheit“, schreibt Bostrom, „erscheint es sinnvoll, das eigene Vertrauen in etwa zu gleichen Teilen auf (1), (2) und (3) zu verteilen“. Kurz gesagt: Man weiß es nicht, aber alles wäre möglich.
Das klingt plausibel – allerdings nur, wenn man die Narrative des Transhumanismus akzeptiert. Die philosophische Community schreckte das nicht ab, denn Bostroms Gedankenexperiment greift uralte philosophische Streitfragen wieder auf: Gibt es eine Realität hinter der Realität, die wir wahrnehmen? Können wir Realität überhaupt erfassen? Gibt es vielleicht sogar „Schöpfer“ der Realität?

articles.title: Como se preparar para não ser substituído pela IA e aumentar seu salário em até 62% • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Resumo
- A revolução da inteligência artificial (IA) já está em curso, transformando diversas áreas do mercado de trabalho, criando novos cargos e salários mais altos; estudos indicam que profissionais com competências em IA podem ter salários até 62% maiores.
- O mercado de trabalho está mudando, com 170 milhões de empregos criados e 92 milhões eliminados até 2030; 59% dos profissionais precisarão de requalificação ou capacitação, e 63% dos executivos citam a falta de qualificação como uma barreira para adotar a IA.
- Para se preparar para o mercado de trabalho na era da IA, é recomendável buscar programas de ensino, como os oferecidos pela TripleTen, que combinam formação prática com acompanhamento de carreira dedicado, para desenvolver competências em IA e áreas relacionadas.
Se você acha que a inteligência artificial é a tecnologia do futuro, talvez esteja enganado: ela já é a tecnologia do presente. Em várias empresas, ferramentas para gerar textos, imagens, documentos, planilhas e apresentações já são realidade. Para quem trabalha com desenvolvimento de software, por exemplo, ela se tornou uma ferramenta essencial para economizar horas de trabalho na escrita de código. Já os agentes capazes de operar por longos períodos assumem sozinhos diversas tarefas.
Essas capacidades técnicas tiveram impacto nas organizações, redesenhando equipes, assumindo funções e criando novos cargos. Em todos os setores, o mercado de trabalho já mudou, e essa é uma ótima notícia. Estar preparado para o novo cenário é a melhor forma de aproveitar grandes oportunidades, com salários mais altos. Estudos apontam, inclusive, que ter competências em IA pode render um salário até 62% maior.
Como a IA está mudando o mercado de trabalho?
As aplicações e os cases de IA nos mais variados segmentos econômicos já dominam palestras, congressos e notícias. Já é comum, em conversas sobre trabalho, ouvir como cada empresa recorre à tecnologia para resolver problemas ou ganhar eficiência.
Pesquisas comprovam o que já vemos no nosso dia a dia: o mercado de trabalho não é mais o mesmo. O relatório Future of Jobs Report 2025, produzido pelo Fórum Econômico Mundial (WEF), estima que 170 milhões de empregos serão criados até 2030, enquanto 92 milhões serão eliminados. Isso quer dizer que haverá um saldo positivo de 78 milhões de empregos.
Alguns desses novos postos de trabalho já começaram a aparecer, e muitos deles pagam mais. A consultoria PwC analisou mais de 1 bilhão de anúncios de emprego em seis continentes. Com isso, ela descobriu que profissionais com competências de IA recebem 62% a mais.
Trabalho não vai faltar, mas é preciso estar preparado desde já. O WEF estima que, de cada 100 pessoas, 59 precisarão passar por requalificação ou capacitação. Entre os executivos, 63% citam a falta de qualificação como uma barreira para adotar a IA. Um levantamento da Kyndryl aponta que 71% dos líderes afirmam que suas equipes ainda não estão preparadas para aproveitar todo o potencial da IA.
Não são só os líderes que se queixam da dificuldade de encontrar profissionais que dominem a IA. Os próprios profissionais reconhecem que também precisam se atualizar. Uma pesquisa da Better Work mostra que 97% dos profissionais não estão satisfeitos com o uso de IA no trabalho e 81% sentem que o mercado está à sua frente. Apenas 3% afirmam dominar a IA em sua área.
O que é possível fazer com a IA?
Ao contrário do que muita gente pensa, as oportunidades envolvendo inteligência artificial não estão restritas a quem atua no setor de tecnologia.
Um levantamento da Lightcast mostra que 56% das vagas relacionadas à inteligência artificial são de outros segmentos do mercado, e esse número vem crescendo ano após ano. É mais uma prova de como essas ferramentas são versáteis e, por isso, vêm transformando várias áreas profissionais.
Em alguns setores, a IA pode ser uma aliada na parte operacional. Ferramentas para gerar textos e imagens, por exemplo, podem acelerar a produtividade, enquanto agentes capazes de operar vários softwares ajudam a automatizar parte do trabalho e melhorar os processos.
Além da parte operacional, que agiliza entregas e libera tempo, a inteligência artificial permite analisar grandes quantidades de dados e encontrar correlações que seriam imperceptíveis para seres humanos. Assim, a tecnologia pode contribuir nas decisões estratégicas, mitigando riscos e indicando caminhos com maior probabilidade de sucesso.
Por fim, o momento também abre oportunidades para quem quer trabalhar no desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial em si, criando soluções sob medida para empresas. Nesse caso, é recomendável desenvolver conhecimento em estatística e machine learning, por exemplo.
O que é preciso saber para trabalhar com IA?
As ferramentas de inteligência artificial estão em constante atualização. Por isso, é preciso usá-las com frequência e manter a curiosidade para explorar suas possibilidades. Como grande parte das interfaces é conversacional, não se trata de decorar comandos, mas de entender como formular um prompt que leve aos resultados desejados.
Também é essencial saber quais são as ferramentas mais adequadas para cada tarefa e em quais partes do fluxo de trabalho elas podem ser integradas. Isso garante ganhos de produtividade sem queda na qualidade, mantendo o fator humano no que realmente importa.
Estar preparado para a IA, no entanto, não significa apenas ter habilidade técnica para operar chatbots e agentes. Com tantas transformações, os ambientes de trabalho estão cada vez mais velozes, e a capacidade humana de julgar e decidir ganhou peso considerável para garantir que a execução saia conforme o esperado.
Segundo a pesquisa Work Trend Index 2026, realizada pela Microsoft, usuários de IA apontaram controle de qualidade (50%) e pensamento crítico para analisar informações (46%) como habilidades importantes. Além disso, 86% tratam a IA como ponto de partida, e não como resposta final, preferindo manter a responsabilidade de ser a cabeça pensante do processo.
Quando se trata de análise e tomada de decisão, a IA usa os dados envolvidos nas atividades da empresa. Saber disso, e entender como as ferramentas recorrem a esses recursos, tornou-se vital em diferentes ocupações.
Por mais que o termo “dados” esteja frequentemente associado ao setor de tecnologia, a verdade é que eles são intrínsecos a praticamente qualquer área de atuação — e ninguém entende melhor esses dados do que quem já trabalha diretamente com aquela função.
Um profissional de marketing conhece as métricas de desempenho das próprias campanhas, enquanto um de RH está familiarizado com indicadores de turnover, por exemplo. Assim, cada um deve estar preparado para fazer as perguntas certas à IA. Isso permite identificar padrões, extrair insights e tomar decisões — sempre interpretando corretamente as respostas e corrigindo possíveis erros.
Como se preparar para o mercado de trabalho na era da IA?
Mesmo com as dicas acima, ainda pode parecer difícil se capacitar para dominar a inteligência artificial no trabalho. Se você sentiu isso, saiba que não está sozinho: um levantamento da Better Work aponta que 32,5% dos profissionais dizem não saber por onde começar e 23,4% afirmam não saber como aplicar a IA à própria área.
Por isso, recorrer a programas de ensino é a forma mais recomendada de se atualizar para essa nova fase do mercado de trabalho. No lugar de um aprendizado meramente intuitivo e fragmentado, um curso oferece a estrutura e a abrangência necessárias para extrair o melhor das novas tecnologias.
A TripleTen é uma ótima opção de formação para esse novo cenário. Uma das principais escolas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, ela combina formação prática com acompanhamento de carreira dedicado. Seus programas têm reconhecimento do MEC, além de certificações de instituições como AWS e Arizona State University. Além disso, a instituição faz parte do Nebius Group, grupo especializado em infraestrutura de IA.
A escola oferece no Brasil três programas de MBA sobre inteligência artificial, cada um voltado a um perfil e objetivo de carreira diferentes.
- O MBA em IA Aplicada para Negócios traz competências para implementar a tecnologia no trabalho atual. O foco é trazer resultados melhores na sua área de atuação, sem precisar mudar de carreira ou aprender a programar. Ele é a melhor opção para quem quer utilizar a tecnologia para melhorar processos, produtividade e decisões.
- O MBA em Data Analytics & AI alia conhecimentos de IA e ferramentas como SQL, Python, Power BI, agentes e webhooks, além de conceitos de estatística. É ideal para quem quer transformar dados em insights, melhorar decisões estratégicas e gerar resultados.
- O MBA em Data Science & AI tem perfil mais técnico e científico, com ênfase nas ferramentas de programação e nos conceitos de estatística, sendo uma trilha mais indicada para quem quer se especializar na área e atuar em cargos voltados a esse tipo de tecnologia.
Como conseguir desconto no MBA em IA da TripleTen?
A transformação do mercado de trabalho pela inteligência artificial já está em curso. Ela abre espaço para quem quer se diferenciar na carreira atual e para quem quer explorar novas áreas. Dominar essas ferramentas é o melhor caminho para conquistar cargos mais altos e salários maiores.
A TripleTen oferece o suporte certo para quem quer se aprofundar nas possibilidades da IA. Agende uma consultoria gratuita para descobrir qual MBA combina com seu momento de carreira e aproveite 50% de desconto até 31/08 com o cupom TECNO50

articles.title: Securing the Infrastructure of Intelligence
articles.text:
AI factories are the defining infrastructure of the AI era — where compute transforms energy and data into intelligence that powers every business, industry and country.
In the AI economy, compute is revenue.
AI factories require a full stack of critical resources: advanced chips, packaging, memory, and networking — as well as land, power and shell.
Just as NVIDIA has used its scale, long-term visibility and supply-chain partnerships to secure critical semiconductor resources, we are now applying that same discipline to secure LPS capacity exclusively for NVIDIA AI factories.
Today, we are partnering with SB Energy to secure LPS capacity at the exceptional PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Portsmouth, Ohio, to host NVIDIA compute. OpenAI will be the tenant.
LPS: The Next Strategic Resource
For the vast majority of NVIDIA customers, securing LPS has long been a part of their infrastructure strategy.
The world’s largest cloud service providers and investment-grade enterprises have balance sheets, infrastructure expertise, and long-term contracts to secure LPS independently. They build and operate AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking, systems and software.
This model will continue to represent most of NVIDIA’s business.
But frontier AI labs are different.
Frontier AI labs have extraordinary demand for training and inference compute, but many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support. They may have strong customer demand and rapidly growing revenue yet still lack the decades-long infrastructure contracts and investment-grade financing capacity needed to secure the AI factory infrastructure independently.
Their growth is increasingly constrained not by algorithms or customer demand, but by the availability of compute.
For these companies, more compute means more intelligence, more products, more users and more revenue. NVIDIA is helping provide the infrastructure that powers this flywheel.
PORTS-Pike: A Site for Generations of NVIDIA Compute
OpenAI will build and operate a world-class AI factory at PORTS-Pike. The AI factory will use NVIDIA’s full-stack DSX AI factory platform, including GPUs, CPUs, networking, and infrastructure software.
The initial deployment is expected to provide 4.25 gigawatts of AI factory capacity. Each generation of NVIDIA AI factory systems deployed at PORTS-Pike could represent approximately 1.5 million NVIDIA GPUs, or approximately $150 billion to $200 billion in NVIDIA revenue. Over 20 years, the site can support multiple upgrade cycles.
This is the essential economic point: the LPS commitment secures a long-lived AI factory site, while the NVIDIA compute inside can be upgraded repeatedly. Each new generation can deliver greater production, more intelligence and better economics.
NVIDIA may also choose to extend the arrangement at PORTS-Pike beyond the initial 4.25 gigawatts to secure the remaining capacity of 3.75 gigawatts.
OpenAI and NVIDIA Expanding Compute Opportunity
More broadly, OpenAI has committed to substantial deployments of NVIDIA AI infrastructure through 2030. OpenAI’s existing and planned commitments represent approximately 12 gigawatts of NVIDIA compute, with an opportunity to expand to approximately 16 gigawatts if NVIDIA extends the PORTS-Pike arrangement beyond the initial 4.25 gigawatts.
At these levels, the opportunity represents roughly $600 billion of NVIDIA compute through 2030.
The Important Questions
What is NVIDIA guaranteeing, and for how long?
NVIDIA is supporting the LPS infrastructure at PORTS-Pike for approximately 4 gigawatts over a 20-year term, securing a site on which NVIDIA compute will be exclusively deployed.
Our support is limited to defined portions of lease and power payments, along with a specified residual-value commitment — not the full cost of the site or all of the tenant’s obligations.
The guarantee will become effective in phases as data centers are placed in service between 2028 and 2030. As OpenAI makes lease payments and capacity comes online, NVIDIA’s remaining exposure declines.
Why is NVIDIA guaranteeing PORTS-Pike?
LPS has become a critical constraint on AI factory deployment. NVIDIA is selectively securing exceptional sites where we can host multiple generations of NVIDIA compute and serve durable customer demand.
The productive life of the site extends through multiple generations of NVIDIA systems, each capable of producing more intelligence and more revenue than the generation before.
Is this circular financing?
No. OpenAI will pay the lease.
NVIDIA uses its scale and long-term visibility to secure PORTS-Pike to host NVIDIA compute. This is the same discipline we apply to supply-chain management: we secure critical inputs when we have visibility into customer demand and when doing so enables long-term productive capacity.
What happens to PORTS-Pike if OpenAI does not use the site in the future?
NVIDIA compute is versatile, fungible and broadly adopted. The capacity can be resold to another qualified tenant across NVIDIA’s global ecosystem of cloud service providers, enterprises, AI labs and startups.
CUDA makes NVIDIA compute more than hardware. It gives developers and NVIDIA engineers a common platform to continually improve installed systems.
CUDA makes NVIDIA compute versatile. Versatility makes it fungible. Fungibility drives utilization and durability — making NVIDIA compute a productive asset: rentable and financeable.
The value of an exceptional site, like PORTS-Pike, is not limited to one customer or one generation of compute. NVIDIA’s standardized platform, broad developer ecosystem and large market of potential users support the ability to redeploy productive capacity over time.
How much LPS will NVIDIA secure?
It will be strategic and disciplined.
Most NVIDIA customers will continue to secure their own LPS. The vast majority of LPS hosting NVIDIA compute will continue to be secured directly by CSPs, enterprises, sovereign AI builders and other customers.
NVIDIA will focus selectively on exceptional sites where visible, durable demand can support multiple generations of NVIDIA compute.
The Infrastructure of Intelligence
PORTS-Pike represents the next step in NVIDIA’s journey.
We began by building accelerated computing chips. We then expanded to systems, networking, CUDA and full-stack AI factories. Today, we are helping secure the critical infrastructure required to build these factories.
NVIDIA is the full-stack AI infrastructure platform.
We are investing in the long-lived foundations of AI factories so our customers can deploy the most productive compute platform in the world, generation after generation.
By securing the critical resources needed to host NVIDIA compute, we can help the world’s most innovative companies build the AI factories that will power the age of intelligence.

articles.title: Ban on Chinese robots leaves U.S. startups stranded
articles.text:
The U.S. government is forcing a rapid onshoring of robotics through a sweeping ban on foreign-made robots, even before an American supply chain exists, putting at risk the very robotics startups the policy is trying to cultivate.
The Federal Communications Commission last month added “advanced robotic devices” to its list of banned devices that pose national security risks. Under the rule, new models of foreign-made humanoids, quadrupeds, and even robot vacuums as well as lawn mowers will be banned from the American market.
To qualify for entry, a robot needs to be assembled in the U.S. and must have at least 65% of its components by value produced domestically. The required share of domestic parts will rise to 75% in 2029. The ban is not targeted at any single country, but is widely seen as aimed at China, which dominates robotics manufacturing.
The policy does not affect devices already being sold in the U.S., and robots imported to support product development, not for sale, will continue to be allowed. Still, startup founders struggle to see how they can manufacture commercial robots without China’s comprehensive electronics supply chain.
Clients and founders share security concerns
“Look at Apple, it’s made in China. How do you expect even more complicated products like robots to be built in America?” Anto Patrex, founder of CosmicBrain AI in San Francisco, told Rest of World. “I have no idea. Till now, we are all figuring it out.”
Patrex’s company aims to make robots that fetch deliveries and carry laundry in apartment buildings. Like most robotics entrepreneurs in the Bay Area, he experimented with Chinese robots and had his first products assembled in China. In early 2026, sensing growing U.S. scrutiny of Chinese robots, Patrex set up an additional assembly facility in Canada, with key components coming from China, meaning these robots wouldn’t qualify for sale in the U.S. under the latest FCC rule.
Elizabeth Williams, the New York-based founder of Gemma, which designs home beauty cosmetics robots that apply makeup for people, told Rest of World her company was also working with a Chinese manufacturer to build its prototypes. “It would have been impossible to do that here,” Williams said. “If we’re not going to work with prototyping and iterating quickly in China, then tell us how you’re going to incentivize manufacturing firms here and robotics founders here.”
American robotics entrepreneurs said they shared the security concerns about Chinese products, but that it would be difficult to meet the stringent made-in-America requirements. Many robotics components are too expensive, too slow to procure, or completely unavailable in the U.S. To get components faster, employees at Silicon Valley companies had even flown from China to the U.S. with robot parts in their suitcases, The Information reported.
Michael Perry, head of commercial strategy at Persona AI, a Houston-based startup that is developing industrial humanoid robots, told Rest of World that even before the FCC ban, U.S. clients had been requesting robots with no Chinese components for security reasons. Perry said Persona AI had been sourcing parts from Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Italy.
But the company still needs to work toward satisfying the latest FCC rule requiring 65% made-in-American components, Perry said. In addition to banning foreign products, he added, the U.S. government should be doing more to grow the domestic supply chains. “You need to provide the carrot as well as the stick,” Perry said. “Right now, you’re only providing the stick.”
How China pulled ahead to dominance
Over the past four decades, as U.S. tech companies outsourced manufacturing to less expensive countries, China took a very different path. Beijing’s state support, a strong engineering talent pipeline, and an abundance of low-cost labor built up the world’s most efficient and comprehensive electronics manufacturing industry — Apple assembles about 80% of iPhones in China and sources many components from the country.
The recent rise of electric vehicles in China has also spurred the growth of industries making sensors, batteries, and actuators, which convert energy into physical motion. These components are also needed for robots. The proximity to manufacturers in southern China has allowed Chinese robot makers to develop prototypes much faster than their international peers.
Chinese robots are now some of the most dexterous and affordable products in the market. In 2025, nearly 90% of all humanoids sold globally were Chinese, according to research firm Omdia. Many American startups and university labs use Unitree robots to conduct experiments and develop robotics software.
The U.S. government has come to view the rise of Chinese robots as a national security threat. The Covered List was created by the Congress in 2021 to give the FCC authority to ban devices that pose national security risks. Foreign-made drones, routers, and products from Chinese telecom equipment makers Huawei and ZTE have previously been added to the list.
In adding robots to the Covered List, the FCC cited security vulnerabilities found in Unitree robots and an incident in which a DJI robot vacuum user accidentally gained access to 7,000 other robots through a system loophole. DJI, China’s leading drone maker, also makes cameras, microphones, and robot vacuums.
Among Washington’s goals is preventing the early success of Chinese robots from developing into a long-term supply chain dependence in the U.S. “The least expensive and easiest time to address a supply chain dependency is right now,” said Adam Chan, senior adviser to FCC chairperson Brendan Carr, on the ChinaTalk podcast. Chan said the ban would incentivize the robotics industry to start moving manufacturing to the U.S.
Companies that wish to import foreign robots can apply for conditional approval, but they must submit an onshoring plan detailing how they plan to establish manufacturing in the U.S.
Support from some startups
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World that a more gradual approach, such as slowly increasing tariffs on Chinese robots and components, would be better at cultivating the American robotics industry. The current ban is too broad and risks burdening startups with the high manufacturing costs, he said. “It can really hold back U.S. robotics innovation,” said Chan.
The FCC has previously banned new foreign-made drones and internet routers from the U.S. market. While older models can still be sold, the Trump administration last week announced new tariffs on drones, which it said would bolster the domestic drone industry and supply chain.
The latest FCC ban has added to growing trade tensions between the U.S. and China. China’s Ministry of Commerce criticized the U.S. for disrupting international trade and “overstretching the national security concept.” In August, Beijing imposed trade restrictions on several American entities and tightened export controls on drones sold to the U.S., citing the FCC decision and a separate blacklisting of Chinese firms over alleged labor abuses in Xinjiang.
Some robot makers have welcomed the import ban, hoping it will protect them from cheaper Chinese competition in the long run.
Agility Robotics, which assembles its warehouse robots in Oregon, said in a statement that the FCC rule was an important step toward addressing the national and economic security concerns posed by foreign robots. The company also advocated for “maintaining access to all of the tools and technologies” to advance robotics research. It couldn’t be determined whether Agility currently sources at least 65% of its components domestically. The company did not respond to an inquiry from Rest of World.
Antonio Li, founder of San Francisco-based Nori Robotics, said the company mostly uses motors and actuators made in Asia, but expects the FCC rule to spur the growth of American suppliers.
Although the FCC ban could “raise some complications with the supply chain,” it is also drawing researchers and customers toward American robot makers, Li said.
“The new ban is going to force all the researchers and software-based companies to buy U.S. instead,” he said. “For us, it’s no doubt a positive thing.”

Ce capteur d’activité présente le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif
Le capteur d’activité Xiaomi Smart Band 9 Pro s'affiche aujourd'hui à 49,99 € chez Xiaomi. C'est actuellement le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif, selon les 9 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Xiaomi continue de casser les prix ! Doté d'un GPS, d'un écran Oled et d'un capteur cardio, son Smart Band 9 Pro s'affiche à seulement 80 €.

Points forts
- Bel écran Oled.
- Cardiofréquencemètre précis.
- GPS au poignet.
Points faibles
- Manque applicatif.
- Pas de paiement au poignet.
- Pas de musique au poignet.
Le Xiaomi Smart Band 9 Pro assure l'essentiel. Ce bracelet propose un bon suivi cardiaque, un GPS et un bel écran Oled, et s'avère pratique au quotidien comme dans les séances sportives. On regrette simplement un système d'exploitation HyperOS trop renfermé sur lui-même, n'autorisant aucune application tierce.

La Xiaomi Smart Band 10 vous permettra de suivre vos notifications, nombre de pas, fréquence cardiaque ou encore votre sommeil, le tout dans un boîtier discret et doté d'un écran Oled agréable à l'œil. Mais tout n'est pas parfait : on regrette ainsi l'absence d'un GPS et d'une puce NFC qui l'auraient rendu encore plus pertinente. Mais à 50 €, ce n'est déjà pas mal.
